# Plannotator **⭐️ NEW:** [Plannotator Inbox](https://plannotator.ai/inbox/) is the missing layer between you and managing multi-agent work. Plannotator is a local, browser-based review surface for AI coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Kiro, Droid, Amp, DeepSeek Harness, and Pi. **It plugs directly into your agent** through its hooks and commands. When the agent proposes a plan, html, or finishes writing code, the work opens in your browser and you mark it up, comment, and send feedback directly to the agent for it to act on it.
### Review documents, plans, and agent messages Annotate plans, specs, messages, html, then send the feedback to your agent.

Demo: Plan review with Pi
### Code Review Review local changes or remote PRs. Comment on diffs, suggest code. Your comments go back to the agent. Works with Git, GitButler, Jujutsu (`jj`), Perforce (`p4`), GitHub, and GitLab.

AI built in: ask AI about anything you're reviewing,
or launch AI reviews that post comments to the diff.

## Annotate HTML Artifacts

## Plannotator Inbox

The Plannotator Inbox is one local window where your agents leave you messages, questions, files, and guided reviews while they keep working. Answer a question with a click, annotate a file, and press Send when you can. Nothing holds an agent session open while you do, and your reply goes back to the session that asked. ``` plannotator inbox ``` Claude Code, Pi, and OpenCode connect through Plannotator's plugins, and your replies arrive as their next turn. Any other agent reaches it over MCP with `plannotator inbox mcp`, and `plannotator inbox --help` is the guide an agent reads. [Watch the demo](https://plannotator.ai/assets/inbox-film.mp4) · [More on the Inbox](https://plannotator.ai/inbox/) · [Docs](https://plannotator.ai/docs/reference/inbox/) ## Herdr Annotate: Plannotator in the Terminal

  

[Herdr Annotate](https://github.com/plannotator/herdr-annotate) brings Plannotator-style review to the terminal: annotate terminal text, review whole Markdown documents and your coding agent's replies inside [Herdr](https://herdr.dev), and send the feedback straight back to the agent as its next message. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Copilot CLI, and Droid replies. Annotations are saved in the Plannotator data directory, so terminal reviews and app reviews compound. ``` herdr plugin install plannotator/herdr-annotate ``` Prefer it standalone? [Plannotator TUI](https://github.com/plannotator/plannotator-tui) powers the document review and runs without Herdr: `brew install plannotator/tap/plannotator-tui`. --- ## Commands On Codex, swap the slash commands for `!plannotator …` (e.g. `!plannotator review`) or the `$plannotator-*` skills. ### Annotate ``` /plannotator-annotate README.md # Local markdown file /plannotator-annotate src/ # Browse and annotate files in a folder /plannotator-annotate https://docs.rs/… # Fetch and annotate any URL /plannotator-annotate report.html --render-html # Render HTML as-is instead of converting /plannotator-last # Annotate the agent's last message ``` Need a realistic document to try? Copy the [product requirements document template and filled example](https://docs.plannotator.ai/templates/product-requirements-document) as Markdown. ### Code review ``` /plannotator-review # Review uncommitted changes /plannotator-review # Review a GitHub pull request /plannotator-review # Review a GitLab merge request plannotator review --gitbutler # Review an active GitButler workspace plannotator review --patch-file reading.diff # Review a static caller-supplied unified diff ``` GitButler users can review the whole workspace, one stack, or one branch layer. See the [GitButler workflow guide](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/workflows/gitbutler). ### Plan mode No command needed. Plan mode is wired in through each harness's hooks. Any time your agent creates a plan, the markdown review surface opens for you. ### CLI ``` plannotator sessions # List active Plannotator sessions plannotator sessions --open 1 # Reopen a session in the browser plannotator archive # Browse saved plan decisions read-only ``` --- ## Privacy and network behavior Plannotator does not collect usage telemetry or analytics. Plans, diffs, annotations, drafts, history, and configuration stay local by default. Each plan review, annotate, archive, share-portal, and code-review app surface checks GitHub for the latest Plannotator release when it loads. This sends no plan or review content and gives the Plannotator project owner no usage analytics, although GitHub receives an ordinary request. There is currently no opt-out setting for the release check. Local Git code review can also query the configured `origin` with `git ls-remote` to detect the default branch and a stale baseline; it does not send the local diff. That remote query runs when the review opens, when the page loads its diff, when you switch the diff type or base (including the "Diff out of date · Refresh" button), and when you press Fetch — never on a timer, so an idle review page makes no network calls. Turn it off entirely with `plannotator review --no-git-remote-check`, `PLANNOTATOR_GIT_REMOTE_CHECK=0`, or `{ "gitRemoteCheck": false }` in `~/.plannotator/config.json`; the compare target then comes from local refs only and the "behind GitHub" banner never appears. Content leaves the local workflow only when a network feature needs it: - URL annotation fetches the requested site, through Jina Reader by default for public pages or directly when Jina is disabled or unavailable. - GitHub and GitLab review uses your authenticated CLI and Git remote to retrieve PR or MR data. - Ask AI and review agents send the selected question and relevant plan, document, repository, or diff context to your configured provider. When Ask AI is answered by the agent session that opened Plannotator ("Ask this session"), the question goes to that session instead. - Sharing sends the complete link to whoever or whatever service you use to deliver it. Encrypted short links upload ciphertext to the paste service. - Workspaces is a separate hosted product, so the open source app's local-storage model does not apply to content placed there. The [privacy policy](https://plannotator.ai/privacy) documents these boundaries and the hosted website and waitlist data. --- ## Link sharing Open source asynchronous link sharing remains available for compatibility but is moving to deprecated support. Workspaces is the primary direction for team sharing. No removal date has been announced.

Legacy link-sharing demo: room.plannotator.ai

Share a plan with a teammate and they can annotate it themselves. Import their feedback and send it straight back to your agent. **Small markdown shares** are compressed into the URL fragment. The fragment is not included in the browser's request to the share portal, but it is not encrypted. Anyone or any messaging service with the complete link can read the shared content. The portal host still receives ordinary request metadata. **Large markdown and raw HTML shares** use a short-link service. The share payload is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before upload, the server stores only ciphertext, and the key is kept in the URL fragment rather than sent in the paste request. Anyone with the complete link can decrypt it. Hosted pastes expire after 7 days. Same model as [PrivateBin](https://privatebin.info/). The paste service is [self-hostable](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/workflows/sharing). Sharing can be disabled entirely with `PLANNOTATOR_SHARE=disabled`. [Workspaces](https://plannotator.ai/workspaces) is the primary path for hosted team collaboration. --- ## Install One installer covers almost every agent. It installs the `plannotator` binary, auto-detects your installed agents, and configures hooks, skills, and slash commands for each: ```bash # macOS / Linux / WSL curl -fsSL https://plannotator.ai/install.sh | bash ``` ```powershell # Windows PowerShell irm https://plannotator.ai/install.ps1 | iex ``` The installer downloads the binary from GitHub Releases. A full install can also contact GitHub for release resolution and agent files, Ataraxy-Labs/sem for the optional `sem` sidecar, and npm for Pi, selected extra skills, or the managed agent-terminal runtime. Pinning `--version` skips only GitHub API release resolution, not the release download. See the [privacy policy](https://plannotator.ai/privacy) for the complete network boundaries. Want just the binary and nothing else? Pass `--minimal` (or export `PLANNOTATOR_MINIMAL=1`) to install only the `plannotator` binary to `~/.local/bin`, skipping every skill, hook, slash command, and per-agent config: ```bash curl -fsSL https://plannotator.ai/install.sh | bash -s -- --minimal ``` Then finish the step for your agent: | Agent | After the installer | Details | |---|---|---| | **Amp** | Copy [`plannotator.ts`](apps/amp-plugin/plannotator.ts) into `~/.config/amp/plugins/`, then `plugins: reload`. Workflows live in the command palette. | [README](apps/amp-plugin/README.md) | | **Claude Code** | `/plugin marketplace add backnotprop/plannotator`, then `/plugin install plannotator@plannotator`. Restart Claude Code. | [README](apps/hook/README.md) | | **Codex** | Nothing. Plan review is enabled automatically via Codex's experimental `Stop` hook (macOS/Linux/WSL; on native Windows, Codex hooks are experimental and the installer prints manual setup steps). `$plannotator-review`, `$plannotator-annotate`, and `$plannotator-last` skills included. | [README](apps/codex/README.md) | | **Copilot CLI** | `/plugin marketplace add backnotprop/plannotator`, then `/plugin install plannotator-copilot@plannotator`. Restart. Plan review activates in plan mode (`Shift+Tab`). | [README](apps/copilot/README.md) | | **DeepSeek Harness** | Add `@plannotator/dsh` on DSH's Plugins page, or run `dsh plugin --profile add @plannotator/dsh`. Plan review opens on `exit_plan_mode`. The plugin adds `/plannotator-review`, `/plannotator-annotate` and `/plannotator-last`, which open without blocking the session. | [README](apps/dsh-plugin/README.md) | | **Droid** | `droid plugin marketplace add https://github.com/backnotprop/plannotator`, then `droid plugin install plannotator@plannotator`. Commands only, no plan interception yet. | [README](apps/droid-plugin/README.md) | | **Gemini CLI** | Nothing. The hook, policy, and slash commands are configured automatically. Requires Gemini CLI 0.36.0+. | [README](apps/gemini/README.md) | | **Kiro CLI** | Nothing. Skills and an example agent are installed automatically. Try `kiro-cli chat --agent plannotator`. | [README](apps/kiro-cli/README.md) | | **OpenCode** | Add `"plugin": ["@plannotator/opencode@latest"]` to `opencode.json`. Restart OpenCode. | [README](apps/opencode-plugin/README.md) | | **Pi** | Skip the installer. Just `pi install npm:@plannotator/pi-extension`. Start Pi with `--plan`, or toggle with `/plannotator-plan-mode`. | [README](apps/pi-extension/README.md) | | **T3 Code** | For Claude threads in T3: run `plannotator t3 --help` and follow its two steps (sign in to T3 once, add the `--t3` MCP entry). Your Inbox replies then arrive in the thread as new turns. | [README](packages/t3-code/README.md) | **Updating:** run the installer again for the binary and slash commands. It also updates an installed Claude Code plugin when the `claude` command is on your PATH (opt out with `--skip-claude-plugin`); otherwise run `claude plugin marketplace update plannotator`, then `claude plugin update plannotator@plannotator`, then restart Claude Code (refreshing the marketplace alone does not update the plugin). Pi: `pi update --extensions` (a plain `pi update` updates only Pi). On Claude Code 2.1.287 or newer, plan review, code review and annotate don't make Claude wait: Claude ends its turn and your decision arrives later as a message. Set `PLANNOTATOR_CLAUDE_MOD=0` to go back to the classic flow. Full walkthroughs live in the [installation docs](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/start/installation). ### Uninstall The safe default removes recognized Plannotator-installed components and keeps your local plans, history, drafts, guides, and settings: ```bash plannotator uninstall ``` Use `--purge` for a full removal of known local Plannotator data as well: ```bash plannotator uninstall --purge ``` Purge requires typing `purge` at the prompt and explains that the data is local-only: it is not stored on a Plannotator server and cannot be recovered. For automation, pass `--yes` (or `-y`); non-interactive removal refuses to run without it. Use `--dry-run` to preview recognized work without making changes. Host integrations are always part of uninstall. If a broken or unavailable host prevents safe cleanup, the command names the blocking plugin manager or configuration, gives exact manual cleanup instructions, and stops before deleting the binary. Complete that cleanup and rerun uninstall. It also keeps the binary when an agent's config file can't be read (another tool's too), or when a hook it did not install still runs Plannotator. The error names the file, the tool, and what to do. A `plannotator-inbox` entry you added yourself, or a Claude Code or Droid plugin installed for one project, is named with how to remove it and does not keep the binary. These mechanics keep the ordinary confirmation default-negative, make the irreversible outcome require a stronger explicit word, and still give package managers and scripts a conventional non-interactive flag. The command covers the conventional macOS, Linux, WSL, and Windows binary locations; the managed `sem` sidecar and agent-terminal runtime; installer skills, commands, hooks, policies, caches, and recognizable Amp/Kiro files; and detected Claude Code, Copilot CLI, Droid, Pi, and VS Code installations through their host CLIs. Shared JSONC settings are edited surgically, while strict JSON updates preserve the file's indentation, line endings, and trailing-newline style. Custom or unrecognized files, separately installed optional skills, project-local integrations, external plan-save locations, and invalid configs are preserved (malformed host config is a fail-safe error). If cleanup reports an error, the CLI remains available for a safe retry, and its Windows PATH entry is retained or restored when possible. If PATH restoration itself fails, the output gives the full CLI path for retry and asks for manual PATH repair. For safety, purge refuses filesystem roots, the home directory, the shared temporary directory, symlinked data directories, and non-directory data paths. Existing paths are compared by filesystem identity, so case aliases, symlinks, hardlinks, and bind mounts cannot bypass the root/home/ancestor checks. That identity and every containment guard are revalidated after awaited host commands, immediately before the synchronous data-removal block; a replaced data directory is refused without touching either the old or replacement data. If your dedicated data directory is symlinked, point `PLANNOTATOR_DATA_DIR` at its resolved target and retry. If you installed only the standalone Pi extension and do not have the `plannotator` CLI, use `pi remove npm:@plannotator/pi-extension`.
Claude Code: manual hook setup (without the plugin system) Add to `~/.claude/settings.json`: ```json { "hooks": { "PermissionRequest": [ { "matcher": "ExitPlanMode", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "plannotator", "timeout": 345600 } ] } ] } } ```
Pin a specific version ```bash curl -fsSL https://plannotator.ai/install.sh | bash -s -- --version vX.Y.Z ``` ```powershell & ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://plannotator.ai/install.ps1))) -Version vX.Y.Z ```
### Try it The fastest way to see what Plannotator does is to invoke it yourself, right now, from your agent: ``` /plannotator-last # annotate the agent's last reply /plannotator-review # review your current diff, PR-style /plannotator-annotate report.html # annotate any file, folder, or URL ``` (Slash commands in most agents; `$plannotator-*` skills in Codex, command palette in Amp.) Plan review needs no command at all. The next time your agent proposes a plan, it opens in your browser automatically. --- ## How it works ### Plan review ``` Agent calls ExitPlanMode -> PermissionRequest hook fires -> Local server reads plan from hook input -> Browser opens with review UI -> You annotate and approve/deny -> Approve: agent proceeds -> Deny: structured feedback sent to agent -> Agent revises, plan diff shows what changed ``` ### Code review ``` You run /plannotator-review -> git diff captures changes (or PR fetched by URL) -> Browser opens with diff viewer -> Annotate lines, stage/unstage files -> Send feedback: returned to agent session -> Approve: "LGTM" sent ``` --- ## Integrations **VS Code**: Open plans in editor tabs, view diffs inline, add annotations from the editor gutter. Install from the [VS Code Marketplace](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=backnotprop.plannotator-webview). **Obsidian**: Auto-save approved plans to a vault with YAML frontmatter, tags from the plan title, and backlinks for graph connectivity. Configure in Plannotator's Settings panel. **Bear**: Save plans as Bear notes with nested tags and project metadata. **Notion**: Save plans as Markdown child pages under a shared Notion page. Set `NOTION_TOKEN` in the environment that starts Plannotator, then configure the parent page in Settings. **GitHub / GitLab**: Pass any PR or MR URL to `/plannotator-review` and review it with the full diff viewer, annotations, and file tree. --- ## Remote / SSH / devcontainer Plannotator auto-detects SSH sessions and switches to fixed port `19432`. For a different port, or in a devcontainer or Docker: ```bash export PLANNOTATOR_REMOTE=1 export PLANNOTATOR_PORT=9999 # forward this port ``` VS Code devcontainers forward the port automatically (check the Ports tab). For raw SSH, add this to `~/.ssh/config`, using your `PLANNOTATOR_PORT` value if you set one: ``` Host your-server LocalForward 19432 localhost:19432 ``` In remote mode the server listens on every interface (`0.0.0.0`) with no login, so anyone who can reach the port can use it, even when you use an SSH tunnel. Keep the port closed to networks you don't trust. --- ## Security Every released binary ships with a SHA256 sidecar. [SLSA provenance](https://slsa.dev/) attestations are available from v0.17.2. The current release workflow also attaches a CycloneDX JSON SBOM, evaluates it with a fresh Grype database before anything is attested or published, and creates a GitHub/Sigstore SBOM attestation for the shipped binaries and npm tarballs. The SBOM is intentionally labeled as a release-wide Syft inventory of the monorepo's locked build inputs and dependencies. It is not an exact per-binary runtime inventory: Bun standalone executables do not expose their bundled JavaScript package metadata to Syft. The canonical [installation and verification docs](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/start/installation#pin-or-verify-a-release) cover the existing installer path; the exact new SBOM commands are included below and must be copied to that Mintlify page before the first SBOM-enabled release. The release gate rejects scanner-side ignored matches and treats unknown applicability conservatively as runtime when evaluating CISA KEV and fixable Critical findings. Its explicit Grype configuration, complete JSON results, database status, and repository policy decision remain available as workflow evidence. # dsh-ssh-helper

给 AI 运维个人服务器用的 SSH 连接池、8 个工具和一道防止误删系统的护栏。同一套核心有两种接入方式：**DSH 插件**，或标准的 **MCP server**（stdio，任何 MCP 客户端或网关都能接入）。

- **连接复用**：每台主机一个常驻 SSH 连接，断线自动重连，命令不再重复握手。
- **会话隔离**：`cd` 和环境变量按调用方隔离，连接共享。
- **安全护栏**：只拦会让整台机器报废的 6 类操作，其余放行。
- **key-only**：使用 `~/.ssh/config` 里的密钥或 ssh-agent，不支持密码，也不存私钥。

```
lib/              共享核心：连接池、策略、工具、面板 API
ui/               共享面板界面：<ssh-helper-panel> 元素 + 纯渲染函数（DSH 与 MCP 共用）
index.js  client.js  dsh/   DSH 适配层（插件注册、计划模式拦截；client.js 只负责把面板放进 DSH）
mcp/      bin/            MCP 适配层（stdio server + 管理面板）
```

## 安装

前置：Node.js ≥ 22，`~/.ssh/config` 里已配好主机。

### 方式一：DSH 插件

```bash
git clone https://github.com/bcdws/dsh-ssh-helper.git
cd dsh-ssh-helper
npm install
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add "link:$PWD"
```

用 `dsh plugin --profile <profile> list` 确认已加载；`ssh_hosts` 的结果里出现 `[policy]` 也说明已加载。

### 方式二：MCP server

不需要 clone。把下面这段配置加到你的 MCP 客户端或网关里（Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 等都用同一段）：

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ssh": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "github:bcdws/dsh-ssh-helper#stable"]
    }
  }
}
```

需要时可以在 `args` 末尾追加参数：`--config <file.json>`（与插件 config 同名的键，如 `hosts`、`exclude`、`autoConnect`；设置 `"autoConnect": true` 或主机别名数组后，server 启动时会在后台预先建好连接）、`--ssh-config <path>`、`--state <path>`、`--no-control`、`--quiet`。

#### 管理面板

```bash
npx -y github:bcdws/dsh-ssh-helper#stable panel --open
```

在 `http://127.0.0.1:7318/` 打开管理页面。它和 DSH 侧边栏是同一个 `<ssh-helper-panel>` 界面（`ui/`），布局、文案和交互只维护一份。面板只在这个终端开着时运行。

- 7318 已经有本机的面板在运行时，直接复用它（`--open` 会打开它），不会再起一个。
- 7318 被别的程序占用时，自动改用下一个空闲端口，并打印出实际地址。用 `--port` 指定的端口被占用时会直接报错。
- Windows 和 WSL 各开各的面板：每个面板只管自己这一侧（自己的 `~/.dsh-ssh-mcp/` 和 `~/.ssh/config`），只能看到同一侧的 MCP 进程。WSL 开了镜像网络时两边共用端口，后启动的那个会认出对方不是自己这一侧的面板，自动换端口。在 WSL 里用 `--open` 会用 Windows 的浏览器打开。

页面上可以管理：

- 主机以固定宽度的卡片列出，空间够时一行三张，不够自动换行；地址、密钥、状态、生产/隐藏开关、单独的空闲超时、备注、最近失败和会话都直接显示，不用点开侧栏；
- 主机的隐藏、生产（prod）标记、备注、单独的空闲超时，以及输出上限、空闲超时、传输超时、日志旁路分析、地址打码这几项全局设置；地址打码会把地址显示成马赛克块，只影响面板显示，截图前打开即可，不用再手动涂抹；
- 重命名 Host 和密钥文件（会修改 `~/.ssh/config`，并先备份）；
- 本机所有正在运行的 MCP 进程（每个客户端会话一个）及其实时连接，可以手动连接或断开。

工作方式：

- 设置保存在 `~/.dsh-ssh-mcp/state.json`，**只有面板写这个文件**，每个 MCP 进程只读跟随，大约 1 秒内生效。隐藏一台主机后，agent 立即失去访问，各进程到它的现有连接会在 20 秒后自动断开（给正在跑的命令留出收尾时间）；20 秒内恢复可见就不会断开。
- 每个 MCP 进程启动后会在 `127.0.0.1` 的随机端口上开一个控制口，并把端口和令牌写进 `~/.dsh-ssh-mcp/run/<pid>.json`（权限 0600），面板通过这个文件找到它。不需要面板时可以加 `--no-control`。
- 面板和控制口都只接受本机请求，并且会校验 `Host` 头（防 DNS rebinding）；写操作还需要令牌。面板自己不会建立 SSH 连接。
- `DSH_SSH_MCP_HOME` 可以把上面这个目录换到别处。

**更新**：`stable` 分支只在 CI 全部通过后才前进；npx 每次启动都会重新解析它，所以新版本在下次启动 server 时自动生效，不用重装。想固定版本就把 `#stable` 换成 tag（如 `#v0.6.0`），想跟最新提交就去掉 `#stable`。

这个包运行时零依赖（ssh2 已预打包进 `vendor/`），npx 只解一个 tarball、不跑安装脚本，启动足够快，不会超出客户端等待 `initialize` 的时间。

两种方式互不影响：

- 各有各的连接池和状态文件：MCP 默认跟随自己的 `~/.dsh-ssh-mcp/state.json`，不读 DSH 面板的状态。如果想让它跟随 DSH，加 `--state ~/.dsh/ssh-pool/state.json`（只读）；这时 MCP 面板里的隐藏和设置对这个进程不生效，面板会标出来。
- 在 DSH 面板里隐藏主机，只影响 DSH 的连接池；在 MCP 面板里隐藏主机，只影响跟随 MCP 状态文件的进程。
- 已经装了插件的 DSH agent 不要再接这个 MCP，否则工具会重复。

## 工具

| 工具 | 用途 |
|---|---|
| `ssh_hosts` | 列主机、连接状态、最后错误 |
| `ssh_run` | 执行命令；`session` 保持目录和变量，`background` 后台运行 |
| `ssh_read` / `ssh_grep` / `ssh_glob` | 读文件、搜内容、找文件 |
| `ssh_write` / `ssh_edit` | 写新文件 / 精确修改现有文件 |
| `ssh_transfer` | 上传或下载单个文件 |

### 生产服务器标记与失败诊断

- **prod 标记**：在面板里给主机打开「生产」开关，标记会存进状态文件。它不拦截任何命令，只是提醒：`ssh_hosts` 里这台主机会带 `[PROD]`；对它调用 `ssh_run` / `ssh_write` / `ssh_edit` / `ssh_transfer` 时，结果第一行都会提醒 agent 先说明影响、取得确认，再重启、删除或修改配置和数据。
- **主机备注**：面板卡片上的备注会进入 agent 上下文——`ssh_hosts` 里显示为 `note=…`，并且对这台主机的每次工具调用结果都会带上 `[note] <alias>: <备注>`，agent 不用先列主机也能知道这台机器是做什么的。
- **错误码**：工具失败时，错误信息末尾会附一行 `[error: <code>] 下一步建议`。MCP 还会把它放进 `_meta["dsh-ssh-helper/error"]`（`failureCode` / `hint` / `retryable`）。目前的错误码有：`connect_timeout`、`connection_refused`、`host_unreachable`、`auth_failed`、`key_unusable`、`host_key_mismatch`、`transport_lost`、`exec_timeout`、`cancelled`、`policy_denied`、`unknown_host`、`local_path`、`invalid_argument`。
- **失败记录**：失败、超时或被客户端取消的调用，都会记到这台主机的 `lastFailure`（工具、错误码、信息、发生在几秒前）和 `callFailures` 上，`ssh_hosts` 和面板里都能看到。`failures` / `lastError` 仍然只统计建连本身。
- **本机信息**：`ssh_hosts` 会返回 `local`，即 MCP server 所在机器的 hostname、OS、cwd 和已运行时长。`ssh_transfer` 的 `localPath` 是按这台机器解析的。如果客户端报了超时，而 `local.uptimeSeconds` 很小，说明 server 是刚启动的，那次超时多半发生在启动阶段（比如 npx 拉取代码），请求并没有到达 server。
- `lastCommandSeconds` 更名为 `lastCommandAgeSeconds`（意思是距上次命令过去了多少秒），旧字段保留一个版本。

## 安全边界

**这不是沙箱。** 护栏只拦 6 类致命操作：递归删除系统目录、`mkfs` / 分区、`dd` 写块设备、覆盖设备或系统关键文件、递归改系统目录权限、`cd` 到系统目录后批量删除。业务目录（`/srv`、`/home`、`/opt`、`/var/www`、`/data`）不拦。两种方式都在工具内部执行这道检查。

- 被拒时应说明意图（哪台机器、做什么、预期影响），不要换一种等价写法重试。误报按 bug 处理。
- 计划模式拦截和本地 bash 拦截只在 DSH 里有。在 MCP 下，审批由客户端负责：工具带有只读 / 可能破坏的注解。
- 真正可靠的保障在插件之外：远程用非 root 账号加 sudo 白名单，重要数据做快照或异机备份。
- 日志旁路分析默认关闭。开启后日志先脱敏再交给模型（DSH 用默认模型，MCP 用客户端的 sampling）；超过 64 KB 时不再只截前一段，而是优先抽取错误/警告行及其上下文，再用开头和结尾补足，省略处有 `[... 行省略 ...]` 标记。
- MCP 客户端没有声明 `sampling`（例如 magpie）时，不再只返回预览，而是给一份本地规则摘要：错误签名 Top 8、次数、首末时间、首末问题行和末尾 8 行。它不调用模型、文本不出本机，输出会标注“本地规则摘要（无模型）”。

## 开发

```bash
node test/run.mjs --offline   # 离线测试，不需要服务器
node test/run.mjs             # 加上可选的 live 测试
```

推送到 `main` 后 CI 跑测试和打包冒烟，全绿则自动把 `stable` 快进到该提交；推 `v*` tag 会生成带 tarball 的 release。

## License

MIT

No candidate code or lifecycle hooks were executed; runtime safety and compatibility are unproven.

evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# Activity indicator

A thin bar that shows what the model and its helpers are doing right now: reading the prompt, thinking, writing, running tools, searching the web, or working in the background. It works the moment it is installed; there is nothing to set up.

It can also play a sound when it needs you. It keeps no text of your conversations, writes no file and sends nothing anywhere. It only counts, times and names tools, in memory.

## What it shows

| Kind | Short code | What it means | Figures |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Prompt processing | PP | the request was sent and no token has come back yet | seconds so far, size of the conversation, the last measured speed |
| Thinking | Thinking | reasoning tokens are arriving | tokens per second, seconds |
| Token generation | TG | the answer, or a tool call's arguments, is being written | tokens per second, tokens so far |
| Tool calls | Tool | a tool is running | the tool's name, seconds, how many |
| Web search | Web | a web search or fetch tool is running | name, seconds |
| Scripts and commands | Run | a shell command or script tool is running | name, seconds |
| Sub-agents | BG | helpers of the conversation on screen are working | how many, for how long |
| Other conversations | OC | another conversation is working | how many |
| Waiting for you | | the app waits for your approval; everything pulses in one colour | which tool, for how long |
| Errors and retries | | a turn failed or the model request is retried; everything pulses red | the reason |

Several things at once are joined with a dot: `TG 42 t/s · Tool read_file 2s · BG 2 · 1m 12s`. While the model thinks or writes, the text can also carry the last prompt speed (`PP 1,850 t/s`) and the size of the conversation (`ctx 12.4k`).

### How the figures are worked out

- **Thinking and writing speed** come from the app's live stream. The app reports text, not tokens, so the indicator counts characters and divides by the characters per token it measured on the last finished request of that conversation (4 until one has finished). The figure is an estimate that corrects itself.
- **Prompt processing speed** is the number of prompt tokens the server actually read (cached ones left out) divided by the time until the first token. It is known when the request finishes, so while a prompt is being read the text shows the seconds so far and the *last* speed.
- **Conversation size** is the token count the model server reported for the last request.

## Designs

Pick one in **Settings → Activity**. The bar always keeps its full length; the text has its own row and is cut short with "…" if it does not fit.

| Design | Where | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pulse line | above the chat box | one line with flowing dots in the colour of what the model is doing |
| Lanes | lower window edge | one hairline per running thing |
| Threads | above the chat box | a rounded lane; each running thing is a thread, several weave into a braid |
| Ticker tape | lower window edge | history: now is at the left, older work drifts right |
| Rings | beside the model button | one small ring per kind of work; an active one spins, faster for faster work and larger for a larger conversation |
| Pulse line + Ticker tape | both | now above the chat box, history on the window edge |
| Threads + Rings | both | how much is going on in the lane, which kinds in the rings |

While a design uses the lower window edge, the app is made that many pixels shorter, so the strip never covers the app's own bottom line.

## Sounds

The indicator can play a short sound when the app starts waiting for your approval and when a turn fails. Retries make no sound.

- Nine sounds to choose from, one for waiting and one for errors: chime, beep, double beep, triple beep, bell, ping, low, alarm, siren. **Try** plays the chosen one.
- **Volume** goes from barely audible to loud.
- **Repeat while it still waits** plays the waiting sound again every 10 seconds to 5 minutes until you answer. The default is once.
- The sounds are made in the app itself; there are no sound files. They follow their own switch, not the "What to track" switches.
- A browser only allows sound after you have clicked or typed in the page once, so in the web version the very first alert after opening the page can be silent.

## Settings

Everything is on **Settings → Activity**, with a preview you can switch through sample states.

- **Look:** on or off, design, thickness, fit the message box, hide when nothing is running, no movement (colour only).
  - **Fit the message box** (`fit`, on by default) makes the line the top part of the message box: the same width, colour, rounded corners and shadow, with no space between them. All of that is read from the box itself, so it follows the window and the colour scheme. While it is joined, the box's own top corners are squared; they are put back when the line is hidden or Fit is off. Off lets the line span the whole chat area, as before 0.27.1.
- **What to track:** a switch and a colour per kind of work. A kind that is switched off disappears from the bar, the rings, the tape and the text.
- **Sounds:** on or off, volume, the sound for waiting, the sound for errors, repeat.
- **Text:** show it or not, figures, words in place of short codes, last prompt speed, conversation size.
- **Ticker tape:** how much history (1, 2, 5 or 15 minutes), solid blocks or ticks, fading, a mark every 10 seconds.
- **Tool names:** which tools count as web search or as a script. A tool counts when its name contains one of your words; empty uses the built-in lists.

`/activity` in a chat says in words what is running.

## For developers

- Server (`index.js`): listens to `session/event` (`turn/start`, `turn/end`, `step/start`, `assistant/message`, `tool/call`, `tool/result`, `approval/asked`, `approval/decided`, `llm/retry-started`) and to `agent/assistant-stream` (frames `start`, `chunk`, `end`; chunks `reasoning-delta`, `text-delta`, `tool-call-delta`). `lib/tracker.js` holds the state; `lib/label.js` builds the text and the sample states.
- Route `GET /dsh-activity/status`; header `x-dsh-session` names the conversation on screen, `x-dsh-demo` asks for a sample state. The answer holds the state, the text and the display settings.
- Service `activity` (apiVersion 1): `snapshot(sessionId?)`, `settings()`.
- Client (`client.js`): slots `conversation.input.dock` (above the chat box), `conversation.input.right` (rings), `shell.overlay` (window edge), `settings.section`. It asks for the status every 0.35 s while something runs and every 0.7 s otherwise (3 s while the window is hidden).

## Checked

- **0.27.2, live in the web profile:** with Fit on, the line sat inside the top of the message box in the box's colour, with the box's corner radius on top, one pixel of overlap and no visible seam, at rest and while a task ran (wave and "Thinking 90.8 t/s"). Switching Fit off gave the box its own corners back and the full-width line; on again rejoined them. Not checked: a light colour scheme, the box while it has the cursor in a scheme that draws a focus ring. In the Mac desktop app the owner confirmed that it looks right.

- **0.27.1, live in the web profile at a 1,500-pixel window:** the line above the message box was 1,213 pixels wide over an 813-pixel box before; with Fit on it has the box's width and place (813 at the same left edge), also on the start page (781) and with the sidebar's Wide chat area on (1,149). Not checked: Fit switched off after the change, a running task at the new width, the Mac app.

- **Unit tests:** 7 (`test/`): a request from prompt to thinking to writing with rates and the prompt speed; tools sorted into tool, web and script; sub-agents and other conversations; waiting, errors and retries; nothing of the conversation's text is kept; the text in every form; settings and where a session sits in the tree.
- **Live, in the throwaway web profile with a slow test model server:**
  - Prompt processing, then thinking, then writing, with rates that matched what the test server sent (about 90 and 60 tokens a second) and a prompt speed of about 3,500 tokens a second for 9,000 tokens in 2.5 s.
  - A `bash` call showed as `Run bash` for its six seconds.
  - A sub-agent showed as `BG 1` on its parent conversation and left when it finished.
  - All seven designs in the settings preview; Pulse line, Ticker tape, Threads and Rings in the real window. The app's bottom line stayed visible above the tape.
  - The Sounds settings; **Try** produced sound output for both sounds (checked by counting the tones the page created, not by ear).
- **Not checked:** the waiting-for-you and error states with a real approval or failure (unit tests and preview only), so the sound was never triggered by a real approval; how the sounds actually sound through speakers; Lanes in the real window; web tools; two conversations at once; the Mac desktop app (the lab is the web version); a real local model.

# DeepSeek Harness Plus

Extra features for the **DeepSeek Harness** desktop app on the Mac: a MindsHub-style sidebar with Chat, Cowork and Code tabs, colour schemes (including MindsHub's navy and teal), work modes, model tiers, a blind model arena, agent swarms, deep research, a usage counter, benchmarks, syncing between Macs and more. Twenty-six add-ons in all, listed in [docs/ADD-ONS.md](docs/ADD-ONS.md).

The add-ons plug into the normal app. Nothing in the app itself is changed, so app updates do not wipe them, and you can remove them at any time.

You do not need to know how to code to install or use this.

---

## What you need

- A Mac with the **DeepSeek Harness** app in your Applications folder, version **0.2.2 or newer, below 0.3**.
- Open the app **once** before installing, so it creates its settings, then quit it.

## Install

1. Download the newest **`DS-Harness-Plus-<version>.dmg`** from the [Releases page](https://github.com/BLCKHWK60/DS-Harness-Plus/releases/latest) and double-click it. A window opens with everything in it: all the add-ons, the installer and this guide. (If you use git, clone the project instead; it is the same folder.)
2. In that window, double-click **`Install.command`**.
   - The first time, macOS may say it "cannot be opened because it is from an unidentified developer". If it does, **right-click** the file, choose **Open**, then **Open** again. You only do this once.
3. A Terminal window opens and walks you through it. If the app is open, it asks to quit it. When it says **Done**, open DeepSeek Harness.

Installing copies the add-ons into the app's own data folder (`~/.dsh/addons`), so you can eject the disk image and delete the download afterwards. To remove the add-ons later, open the disk image again and double-click **`Uninstall.command`**.

Before it changes anything, the installer saves your current setup under `~/.dsh/backups/deepseek-harness-plus/`. If any step fails, it puts everything back by itself.

**Terminal instead:** if you prefer, run this from the unpacked folder:

```bash
bash scripts/install.sh
```

## First steps

1. **Add your models.** Go to **Settings → Models** in the app. You can paste an API key for a provider there, or add your own server (for example a model server on another computer). No files to edit.
2. **Look at the new pages.** **Settings** now has **Colours, Model Tiers, Modes, Sampling, Usage, Benchmark, Arena** and **Swarm** pages. The chat box (where you type) gets one **model button** beside the send button, with the model list, an effort slider from Off to Ultra Code, tiers and sampling, and, once set up, a model-health dot.
3. **Switch on what you want.** Some add-ons work right away. The others do nothing until you give them a little setup, for example which models the arena should compare. [docs/ADD-ONS.md](docs/ADD-ONS.md) says which is which and how to set each one up.

### What works the moment you install

- **Cowork sidebar:** Chat, Cowork and Code tabs at the top of the left sidebar. Each tab lists only its own conversations and projects, and has its own sections: Model Arena under Chat, and Automation tasks, Connectors (your MCP servers, with on/off switches) and Skills under Cowork and Code. The start page gets a greeting and suggestion chips. A tab picks the mode of new conversations, so the chat box no longer needs a mode drop-down. To get the normal sidebar back, switch **Cowork sidebar** off on the **Plugins** page.
- **Colours:** pick a colour scheme in **Settings → Colours**: DeepSeek Harness (the stock colours, the default), MindsHub Cowork, Graphite or Forest, each in light and dark.
- **Modes:** Chat, Cowork and Code modes, switchable per conversation, plus **Search** and **Deep research** buttons in the chat box.
- **Model Tiers:** one model button in the chat box: pick any model and drag the effort slider. Five starter tiers (Fast, Balanced, Deep, Creative, Code review) work at once on whatever model you use. No model is preconfigured.
- **Code map:** a compact map of the project a conversation works in, so the assistant looks things up instead of reading whole files. Plus four "reverse engineer" skills. Nothing to install.
- **Privacy:** switches off the app's usage reporting and the upload of a conversation when you rate an answer. `/privacy` shows the state.
- **Usage counter:** counts requests and tokens per day and model (never your text).
- **Deep research** and **Code power:** new tools and skills the assistant can use.

Everything else stays switched off until you set it up.

## Changing an add-on's settings

Some add-ons have their own page in **Settings** (Tiers, Modes, Sampling). The rest are set up in the app's settings file. To edit it:

1. Quit DeepSeek Harness.
2. In Finder press **⌘ Shift G**, paste `~/.dsh/profiles/desktop/` and press Return.
3. Make a copy of **`cordis.patch.yml`** first, as your own backup. Then open the original with TextEdit.
4. Paste in the block for the add-on you want, from its section in [docs/ADD-ONS.md](docs/ADD-ONS.md). Fill in the parts in `<ANGLE BRACKETS>`, save, and open the app.

The file is indentation-sensitive: use spaces, never tabs, and keep the lines lined up as in the example. If the app will not start after an edit, put your copy back.

## Updating

Download the newer version and double-click **`Install.command`** again. It replaces the add-ons and keeps your settings.

## Removing

Double-click **`Uninstall.command`**. It removes all twenty-two add-ons and their files. Your conversations and your models are not touched. Any settings you wrote for the add-ons stay in the settings file and do nothing; if you install again, they come back into effect.

## Using it on a second Mac

1. Install the DeepSeek Harness app on the other Mac and open it once.
2. Run **`Install.command`** there too.
3. Add your models in **Settings → Models**.
4. Optional: to keep the same **settings** on both Macs, use iCloud Drive (below).
5. Optional: to see the same **conversations** on both Macs, set up the **Sync** add-on (see [docs/ADD-ONS.md](docs/ADD-ONS.md#sync)). It needs a private git repository that both Macs can reach. Neither Mac has to be switched on for the other to sync.

### Same settings on both Macs, through iCloud Drive

The **Shared settings** add-on keeps the settings you change in the app's own pages in one file, `settings.json`, in a folder in iCloud Drive. Those settings are Modes, Model Tiers, the Cowork tabs, Sampling presets and Colours. Change something on one Mac and the other Mac picks it up within about a minute. The file never holds secrets: API keys, tokens and passwords stay on each Mac.

1. On the first Mac, double-click **`Install.command`** and answer **y** when it asks *"Share settings through iCloud Drive?"*. It uses the folder **iCloud Drive → DeepSeek Harness Plus**.
2. On the second Mac, do the same. When the app opens there, it takes the settings from the file. Its own earlier settings are kept in `~/.dsh/shared-settings/backups`.

To use another folder, or from Terminal: `bash scripts/install.sh --settings "<folder>"`. To stop sharing on one Mac: `bash scripts/install.sh --no-settings`. Type `/shared-settings` in a conversation to see what is shared and when it last synced.

**Good to know:**
- Not shared:
  - which conversation sits in which tab;
  - the tier a conversation uses;
  - which add-ons are switched on;
  - settings written by hand into the settings file rather than in a Settings page.
- If you change the same setting on both Macs at once, the copy in iCloud wins. The other value is kept in the backups folder.
- iCloud sometimes makes a copy such as `settings 2.json` when both Macs write at the same moment. `/shared-settings` tells you if one appears; check it, then delete it.

## Giving it to someone else

Send them the link to this project, https://github.com/BLCKHWK60/DS-Harness-Plus. They follow **Install** above. Nothing in here contains your addresses, keys or personal settings; every add-on starts empty.

## If something goes wrong

- **"DeepSeek Harness is not installed"**: the app must be in `/Applications` or `~/Applications`.
- **"No 'desktop' setup found"**: open the app once, quit it, and run the installer again.
- **"version ... works with version 0.2.2 up to 0.3"**: your app is newer or older than this release supports. Look for a newer DeepSeek Harness Plus.
- **The installer stopped with a problem**: it has already put everything back. The message names a log file; send that file to whoever helps you.
- **The app misbehaves after installing**: run **`Uninstall.command`**. Every install and uninstall also leaves a dated copy of your setup files in `~/.dsh/backups/deepseek-harness-plus/`, in case someone helping you needs them.
- **The app will not start after you edited the settings file**: put back the copy you made before editing.

## What is in this folder

| Folder or file | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Install.command`, `Uninstall.command` | Double-click to install or remove. |
| `addons/` | The twenty-two add-ons. Each has a `README.md` with its full technical notes. |
| `docs/ADD-ONS.md` | What each add-on does and how to set it up. |
| `docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md` | For technical readers: how the install works, how to test, how to change an add-on. |
| `templates/` | Optional ready-to-fill examples: model servers, memory, MCP tool servers, backups. |
| `extras/dsh-intel-mcp/` | Optional Python tools (code map, reverse engineering, context store). Needs Python; not installed automatically. |
| `scripts/` | What the `.command` files run. |
| `VERSION` | This release's version number. |
| `LICENSE` | The MIT licence: anyone may use, change and share this. |

## Status

Release 0.29.2 (the version in `VERSION`). Tested so far:

- **Install, update and uninstall:** run on a fresh setup and on a copy of a real, long-used setup.
- **Live start:** the app starts with every add-on loaded.
- **Add-ons:** each has its own automated tests, and each settings page was checked in the app's web version.
- **Not yet tested on another person's Mac.** Each add-on's `README.md` lists what was and was not verified for it.

decision.reason: Held for public installation mapping. MIT repository scope, DSH 0.2.2 engine range and native activity host/client are present. Session/stream subscriptions and settings produce an activity display. The private local add-on name has no npm version; root documentation installs a desktop disk image and copies add-ons, leaving the public standalone bundle mapping unresolved. Other substantive add-ons, including benchmark, are repository duplicates, not templates. No candidate code or lifecycle hooks were executed; runtime safety and compatibility are unproven.

# Agent swarm

Host plugin `@local/dsh-agent-swarm` (dsh 0.2.2-rc.1). One tool, `run_swarm`, runs a **named swarm** of child agents and returns every member's output under its own heading, so the parent's final answer can credit each member. **Nothing is configured by default**: with no swarm the plugin does nothing; a bad definition (too few members, duplicate ids, unknown role, unknown swarm in `defaultSwarmByMode`) fails at load.

## Shapes (`strategy`)

| Strategy | What happens |
|---|---|
| `fanout` | every member works on the task at once |
| `pipeline` | members run in order; each sees a board of the earlier members' outputs (first 600 characters each) |
| `debate` | `rounds` rounds (2 to 5); from round 2 each member sees the others' last answers and revises |

A member is bound to a **role** (`plan`, `implement`, `review`, `fast`): its route is the Tier plugin's role route for the parent's tier (or the member's own `tier`), or an explicit `provider` + `model`. With no usable route it falls back to the parent's route. `instructions` is the member's persona or focus.

## Caps and budget

- **Concurrency**: at most `maxActive` children at once, never above the tier's sub-agent cap or 8 (the dsh default). The tool reports the highest number it actually had running.
- **Depth**: a swarm member cannot start a swarm (dsh's own depth limit is 1 as well).
- **Budget**: `budget.tokens` and `budget.usd` (0 = no cap). Token use is read live from each child's own usage; dollars use your `pricing` map (unlisted models cost 0). When a cap is reached the swarm is cancelled, members that have not answered are reported as such, and the result says why it stopped. Children already running when the cap is crossed finish their current request first, so spend can overshoot a little.
- **Time**: `maxMinutes` per swarm (20 by default).
- The tool is registered with Tier's sub-agent gate, so a tier with sub-agents disabled, or at its cap, refuses it.

## Route health

With the route-health plugin loaded, a member whose route is `down` is handled by `onRouteDown`: `rebind` (default) moves it to the first usable route of the tier's fallback chain and says so in the result; `skip` leaves that member out; `refuse` refuses the whole swarm. If no member can run the tool errors.

## Configuration

```yaml
- id: agent-swarm
  config:
    swarms:
      <NAME>:
        description: '<WHAT IT IS FOR>'
        strategy: fanout            # fanout | pipeline | debate
        rounds: 2                   # debate only
        maxActive: 3                # 1 to 8
        maxMinutes: 20
        budget: { tokens: 0, usd: 0 }
        members:
          - { id: <ID>, role: <plan|implement|review|fast>, instructions: '<FOCUS>' }
          - { id: <ID>, provider: <ROUTE>, model: <MODEL ID>, instructions: '...' }
    pricing: { '<ROUTE>/<MODEL ID>': { inputPerMTok: <USD>, outputPerMTok: <USD> } }
    defaultSwarmByMode: { <MODE ID>: <SWARM NAME> }   # adds a one-line hint to the system prompt in that mode
    onRouteDown: rebind
    toolName: run_swarm
```

## Settings page

Settings > **Swarm** has two cards. **Recent runs** lists the model's last 20 `run_swarm` calls (newest first); pick one to see each member's state (waiting, running, done, failed, skipped, not answered), route, round (debate), tokens and time, plus the run's tokens and dollars against its budget and why it stopped, if it did. It refreshes every 2 seconds while a run is going and every 10 seconds otherwise. **Configured swarms** lists your swarms with members, caps and budget. It is read-only: it cannot start, stop or change a swarm.

It reads one fenced, GET-only route of the host half, `GET /dsh-agent-swarm/state` (login cookie and Host/Origin check). Run records live in the host's memory (the last 20) and are **gone after a host restart**. The route carries no task text, no prompts and no member answers (a unit test searches the JSON for them); a failed member's error line is cut to 160 characters and is the provider's own message. With no swarm configured the tool is not registered, but the route still answers so the page can say so. Needs one app restart to load.

Host change: `execute()` now keeps a small record per run (member states, round, child ids for token sums). 12 unit tests (`node --test test/swarm.test.mjs`): fence and GET-only, no leaked text, live states under a concurrency cap of 1, token budget stop, dollar spend, a failing member, the `skip` policy, debate rounds, the 20-run cap, validation and cost.

Tested in a throwaway web profile with mock models whose replies are delayed 7 seconds, through the real `run_swarm` tool: the page was read while a fan-out ran (members went waiting, running, done with at most 2 at once), while a debate was in round 2, and after a 20-token budget stopped a run (36 of 20 tokens, as documented, with the third member "not answered"). Dark and light theme and a 420-pixel width were looked at. **Not tested:** real models, the desktop app, a swarm with a `rebind` or `refuse` route-down policy on the page (only the unit test covers `skip`), a failing child in a real run, and a host restart while a run is going.

## Not done

- **A shared task board** in the sense of members editing a common list: here the board is the earlier outputs passed to later members (pipeline and debate); fan-out members cannot see each other.
- **Using dsh's `workflow` tool or Agent Teams** (experimental): children are started directly, like Tier's `delegate_role`.
- **A card inside the conversation** for the swarm: a plugin outside the dsh repository cannot add events to a session, and the transcript is built from them. The live view is a Settings page instead (next section).
- Members share the parent's workspace; two members editing the same file can collide. The prompts ask for concise answers, not edits.

## Verified (rc.1, scripted mock model with delayed replies, throwaway home)

Fan-out with `maxActive` 3 and 2: the mock saw at most 3 and 2 requests in flight, and each role used its Tier route (plan on the small model, implement and review on the large one); pipeline members saw earlier outputs; debate ran two rounds; a 30-token budget stopped the swarm after the second member with the third reported as not answered (36 tokens counted); with the primary route reported down the members were re-bound to the fallback route and the result said so; `onRouteDown: refuse` refused the swarm; a tier with sub-agents disabled refused the tool. Unit checks cover validation, cost and the state route.

## Not verified

Real models and real parallel load; very large swarms (above 8 members the cap queues the rest); the `skip` policy; the `defaultSwarmByMode` hint; a swarm member calling the tool (guard only); behaviour when a child fails mid-run beyond the error line.

# DeepSeek Harness Plus

Extra features for the **DeepSeek Harness** desktop app on the Mac: a MindsHub-style sidebar with Chat, Cowork and Code tabs, colour schemes (including MindsHub's navy and teal), work modes, model tiers, a blind model arena, agent swarms, deep research, a usage counter, benchmarks, syncing between Macs and more. Twenty-six add-ons in all, listed in [docs/ADD-ONS.md](docs/ADD-ONS.md).

The add-ons plug into the normal app. Nothing in the app itself is changed, so app updates do not wipe them, and you can remove them at any time.

You do not need to know how to code to install or use this.

---

## What you need

- A Mac with the **DeepSeek Harness** app in your Applications folder, version **0.2.2 or newer, below 0.3**.
- Open the app **once** before installing, so it creates its settings, then quit it.

## Install

1. Download the newest **`DS-Harness-Plus-<version>.dmg`** from the [Releases page](https://github.com/BLCKHWK60/DS-Harness-Plus/releases/latest) and double-click it. A window opens with everything in it: all the add-ons, the installer and this guide. (If you use git, clone the project instead; it is the same folder.)
2. In that window, double-click **`Install.command`**.
   - The first time, macOS may say it "cannot be opened because it is from an unidentified developer". If it does, **right-click** the file, choose **Open**, then **Open** again. You only do this once.
3. A Terminal window opens and walks you through it. If the app is open, it asks to quit it. When it says **Done**, open DeepSeek Harness.

Installing copies the add-ons into the app's own data folder (`~/.dsh/addons`), so you can eject the disk image and delete the download afterwards. To remove the add-ons later, open the disk image again and double-click **`Uninstall.command`**.

Before it changes anything, the installer saves your current setup under `~/.dsh/backups/deepseek-harness-plus/`. If any step fails, it puts everything back by itself.

**Terminal instead:** if you prefer, run this from the unpacked folder:

```bash
bash scripts/install.sh
```

## First steps

1. **Add your models.** Go to **Settings → Models** in the app. You can paste an API key for a provider there, or add your own server (for example a model server on another computer). No files to edit.
2. **Look at the new pages.** **Settings** now has **Colours, Model Tiers, Modes, Sampling, Usage, Benchmark, Arena** and **Swarm** pages. The chat box (where you type) gets one **model button** beside the send button, with the model list, an effort slider from Off to Ultra Code, tiers and sampling, and, once set up, a model-health dot.
3. **Switch on what you want.** Some add-ons work right away. The others do nothing until you give them a little setup, for example which models the arena should compare. [docs/ADD-ONS.md](docs/ADD-ONS.md) says which is which and how to set each one up.

### What works the moment you install

- **Cowork sidebar:** Chat, Cowork and Code tabs at the top of the left sidebar. Each tab lists only its own conversations and projects, and has its own sections: Model Arena under Chat, and Automation tasks, Connectors (your MCP servers, with on/off switches) and Skills under Cowork and Code. The start page gets a greeting and suggestion chips. A tab picks the mode of new conversations, so the chat box no longer needs a mode drop-down. To get the normal sidebar back, switch **Cowork sidebar** off on the **Plugins** page.
- **Colours:** pick a colour scheme in **Settings → Colours**: DeepSeek Harness (the stock colours, the default), MindsHub Cowork, Graphite or Forest, each in light and dark.
- **Modes:** Chat, Cowork and Code modes, switchable per conversation, plus **Search** and **Deep research** buttons in the chat box.
- **Model Tiers:** one model button in the chat box: pick any model and drag the effort slider. Five starter tiers (Fast, Balanced, Deep, Creative, Code review) work at once on whatever model you use. No model is preconfigured.
- **Code map:** a compact map of the project a conversation works in, so the assistant looks things up instead of reading whole files. Plus four "reverse engineer" skills. Nothing to install.
- **Privacy:** switches off the app's usage reporting and the upload of a conversation when you rate an answer. `/privacy` shows the state.
- **Usage counter:** counts requests and tokens per day and model (never your text).
- **Deep research** and **Code power:** new tools and skills the assistant can use.

Everything else stays switched off until you set it up.

## Changing an add-on's settings

Some add-ons have their own page in **Settings** (Tiers, Modes, Sampling). The rest are set up in the app's settings file. To edit it:

1. Quit DeepSeek Harness.
2. In Finder press **⌘ Shift G**, paste `~/.dsh/profiles/desktop/` and press Return.
3. Make a copy of **`cordis.patch.yml`** first, as your own backup. Then open the original with TextEdit.
4. Paste in the block for the add-on you want, from its section in [docs/ADD-ONS.md](docs/ADD-ONS.md). Fill in the parts in `<ANGLE BRACKETS>`, save, and open the app.

The file is indentation-sensitive: use spaces, never tabs, and keep the lines lined up as in the example. If the app will not start after an edit, put your copy back.

## Updating

Download the newer version and double-click **`Install.command`** again. It replaces the add-ons and keeps your settings.

## Removing

Double-click **`Uninstall.command`**. It removes all twenty-two add-ons and their files. Your conversations and your models are not touched. Any settings you wrote for the add-ons stay in the settings file and do nothing; if you install again, they come back into effect.

## Using it on a second Mac

1. Install the DeepSeek Harness app on the other Mac and open it once.
2. Run **`Install.command`** there too.
3. Add your models in **Settings → Models**.
4. Optional: to keep the same **settings** on both Macs, use iCloud Drive (below).
5. Optional: to see the same **conversations** on both Macs, set up the **Sync** add-on (see [docs/ADD-ONS.md](docs/ADD-ONS.md#sync)). It needs a private git repository that both Macs can reach. Neither Mac has to be switched on for the other to sync.

### Same settings on both Macs, through iCloud Drive

The **Shared settings** add-on keeps the settings you change in the app's own pages in one file, `settings.json`, in a folder in iCloud Drive. Those settings are Modes, Model Tiers, the Cowork tabs, Sampling presets and Colours. Change something on one Mac and the other Mac picks it up within about a minute. The file never holds secrets: API keys, tokens and passwords stay on each Mac.

1. On the first Mac, double-click **`Install.command`** and answer **y** when it asks *"Share settings through iCloud Drive?"*. It uses the folder **iCloud Drive → DeepSeek Harness Plus**.
2. On the second Mac, do the same. When the app opens there, it takes the settings from the file. Its own earlier settings are kept in `~/.dsh/shared-settings/backups`.

To use another folder, or from Terminal: `bash scripts/install.sh --settings "<folder>"`. To stop sharing on one Mac: `bash scripts/install.sh --no-settings`. Type `/shared-settings` in a conversation to see what is shared and when it last synced.

**Good to know:**
- Not shared:
  - which conversation sits in which tab;
  - the tier a conversation uses;
  - which add-ons are switched on;
  - settings written by hand into the settings file rather than in a Settings page.
- If you change the same setting on both Macs at once, the copy in iCloud wins. The other value is kept in the backups folder.
- iCloud sometimes makes a copy such as `settings 2.json` when both Macs write at the same moment. `/shared-settings` tells you if one appears; check it, then delete it.

## Giving it to someone else

Send them the link to this project, https://github.com/BLCKHWK60/DS-Harness-Plus. They follow **Install** above. Nothing in here contains your addresses, keys or personal settings; every add-on starts empty.

## If something goes wrong

- **"DeepSeek Harness is not installed"**: the app must be in `/Applications` or `~/Applications`.
- **"No 'desktop' setup found"**: open the app once, quit it, and run the installer again.
- **"version ... works with version 0.2.2 up to 0.3"**: your app is newer or older than this release supports. Look for a newer DeepSeek Harness Plus.
- **The installer stopped with a problem**: it has already put everything back. The message names a log file; send that file to whoever helps you.
- **The app misbehaves after installing**: run **`Uninstall.command`**. Every install and uninstall also leaves a dated copy of your setup files in `~/.dsh/backups/deepseek-harness-plus/`, in case someone helping you needs them.
- **The app will not start after you edited the settings file**: put back the copy you made before editing.

## What is in this folder

| Folder or file | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Install.command`, `Uninstall.command` | Double-click to install or remove. |
| `addons/` | The twenty-two add-ons. Each has a `README.md` with its full technical notes. |
| `docs/ADD-ONS.md` | What each add-on does and how to set it up. |
| `docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md` | For technical readers: how the install works, how to test, how to change an add-on. |
| `templates/` | Optional ready-to-fill examples: model servers, memory, MCP tool servers, backups. |
| `extras/dsh-intel-mcp/` | Optional Python tools (code map, reverse engineering, context store). Needs Python; not installed automatically. |
| `scripts/` | What the `.command` files run. |
| `VERSION` | This release's version number. |
| `LICENSE` | The MIT licence: anyone may use, change and share this. |

## Status

Release 0.29.2 (the version in `VERSION`). Tested so far:

- **Install, update and uninstall:** run on a fresh setup and on a copy of a real, long-used setup.
- **Live start:** the app starts with every add-on loaded.
- **Add-ons:** each has its own automated tests, and each settings page was checked in the app's web version.
- **Not yet tested on another person's Mac.** Each add-on's `README.md` lists what was and was not verified for it.

# Automations

Plugin `@local/dsh-automations` (dsh 0.2.2-rc.2). Answers "did my scheduled tasks work, and does anything need me?" in one place, and tells you on this Mac and on your phone.

The app's own scheduler (the **Automation tasks** page) records only that a task's instruction reached a conversation. To learn how it went you open the conversation. This add-on follows each run to its end and records the result.

It only watches. It never answers for you, changes a task or touches a conversation. The one thing it starts is a task you ask it to run.

## The Automation runs page

In the Cowork sidebar, under **Automation tasks**. It has three parts.

- **Needs you.** Runs that wait for your approval, your answer to a question, or your review of a plan. **Open** takes you to the conversation.
- **Your tasks.** Each scheduled task with its next run and how its last run ended. **Run now** starts it. Tasks that have ended and have no recorded run are left out.
- **Last runs.** Newest first: how it ended, when it started, how long it took, steps and tokens, and the end of the answer (click it to see more). **Open** shows the conversation. A run that failed or was stopped has **Run again**.

How a run can end:

| Shown as | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Finished | The turn completed |
| Failed | The model or a tool gave an error (the reason is shown), the answer was cut off at the model's output limit, or the app closed before the run finished |
| Stopped | A limit or a rule ended it before it finished, for example the Budget guard |
| Cancelled | You stopped it |
| Running, Needs you | Still going |

Runs are recorded from the moment the add-on is installed. Earlier ones are not listed. The last 200 are kept.

## Alerts

**Settings → Alerts.** A short line when a task fails, needs you or finishes.

- **Alert me when:** a task failed or was stopped (on), a task needs me (on), a task finished (off).
- **For which tasks:** scheduled tasks always. Conversations you start yourself only if you switch that on, and then only when the task has run at least the minutes you set (2 unless changed), so quick answers at your desk stay quiet.
- **Where:** on this Mac (on) and on your phone (off until set up).
- **Send a test alert** sends one sample to every place that is on and says what happened.

What the line says: fixed words plus one name. For a scheduled task the name is the task's own, for example `Morning brief failed` or `Weekly review has a question for you`. For a conversation you started it is the project folder, for example `A task in my-site finished`. It never contains your instruction or the answer.

### On this Mac

A normal notification, shown through macOS's own `osascript`. The first time, macOS may ask whether "Script Editor" may show notifications.

### On your phone

Through [ntfy](https://ntfy.sh), a free service with a free app. No account is needed.

1. Install the app "ntfy" on your phone.
2. On the Alerts page, press **Make one up** next to Topic.
3. In the phone app, tap +, type the same topic, and subscribe.
4. Switch on **On my phone** and press **Send a test alert**.

The topic is the name your phone listens to. Anyone who knows it can read your alerts, which is why it should be long and odd, and why the alerts carry only a name and what happened. A topic may have letters, digits, `-` and `_`, up to 64 characters.

## Settings

```yaml
- id: automations
  config:
    enabled: true          # off records nothing and alerts nothing
    alertFailed: true
    alertNeeds: true
    alertFinished: false
    alertOthers: false     # also conversations you start yourself
    othersMinutes: 2       # ...only when the task has run at least this long
    mac: true
    phone: false
    ntfyServer: https://ntfy.sh
    ntfyTopic: ''
```

## How it works

- It listens to the app's session events. A user message whose source is the scheduler and whose text starts with `[SCHEDULE REMINDER` starts a run; the task ids are read from that text. A change notice from the scheduler starts no run.
- `step/start` counts steps and `assistant/message` carries the token usage and the answer's words. A helper agent's work is counted under the conversation that started it.
- Waiting: `approval/asked` (until `approval/decided`), and a call to `ask_user_question` or `exit_plan_mode` (until that call's result).
- `turn/end` closes the run with the app's own reason: `completed`, `error`, `aborted`, `blocked` or `max-tokens`.
- Task names, the task list and Run now come from the app's `schedule` service (`catalog`, `run`).
- The record is `<app data folder>/automations/runs.json`. It holds task names, times, counts and up to 400 characters from the end of each answer.
- Phone alerts are one JSON `POST` to the ntfy server's root, with an 8-second limit. At most 10 alerts go out in a minute.

## Good to know

- Tasks run only while the app is running. It keeps running in the menu bar when the window is closed. Nothing runs while the Mac sleeps, and this add-on does not change that.
- Phone alerts pass through the ntfy service, which can read them. The free service allows 250 messages a day.
- The topic is saved with the app's other settings on this Mac, as plain text.
- You cannot answer from the phone. Open the app to approve or reply.
- The older **Notify** add-on still works beside this one. It runs a command you write; this needs no command.

## Not built yet

- Per-task settings: its own mode, what it may do without asking, its own limits.
- Ending a run that has waited too long for an answer.
- An alert when a task has not succeeded for a set number of hours.

## Code

`lib/runs.js` (the record; tested in `test/runs.test.mjs`), `lib/alerts.js` (the line, the settings, the two senders, the rate limit; tested in `test/alerts.test.mjs`), `index.js` (events, the scheduler, the `GET/POST /dsh-automations/data` route), `client.js` (the two pages).

## Tested

In the lab (web version, stand-in model, a stand-in for the ntfy server): the page listed the tasks; **Run now** started a run that showed Running and then Finished with its time, steps, tokens and words; a run whose model returned an error showed Failed with the reason, and **Run again** started a new run; a run that asked a question showed under Needs you, **Open** opened it, and after the answer it went on and finished. Each of these sent the right alert. The Alerts page saved every setting and kept them over a restart; a bad topic and a refusing server were reported in plain words; with alerts for my own conversations on, a finished and a failed one each sent an alert. A test alert through `osascript` ran without error on macOS.

Not tested: the real ntfy service and a real phone; whether the Mac notification is visible (only that the command succeeded); the waiting kinds "approval" and "plan review" (unit tests only); a task run by its schedule instead of Run now; helper agents; the app closing mid-run (unit test only). In the Mac desktop app the owner confirmed that the page and the alerts work; nothing more detailed was checked there.

The chat box (where you type) gets one **model button** beside the send button, with the model list, an effort slider from Off to Ultra Code, tiers and sampling, and, once set up, a model-health dot.
3. **Switch on what you want.** Some add-ons work right away. The others do nothing until you give them a little setup, for example which models the arena should compare. [docs/ADD-ONS.md](docs/ADD-ONS.md) says which is which and how to set each one up.

### What works the moment you install

- **Cowork sidebar:** Chat, Cowork and Code tabs at the top of the left sidebar. Each tab lists only its own conversations and projects, and has its own sections: Model Arena under Chat, and Automation tasks, Connectors (your MCP servers, with on/off switches) and Skills under Cowork and Code. The start page gets a greeting and suggestion chips. A tab picks the mode of new conversations, so the chat box no longer needs a mode drop-down. To get the normal sidebar back, switch **Cowork sidebar** off on the **Plugins** page.
- **Colours:** pick a colour scheme in **Settings → Colours**: DeepSeek Harness (the stock colours, the default), MindsHub Cowork, Graphite or Forest, each in light and dark.
- **Modes:** Chat, Cowork and Code modes, switchable per conversation, plus **Search** and **Deep research** buttons in the chat box.
- **Model Tiers:** one model button in the chat box: pick any model and drag the effort slider. Five starter tiers (Fast, Balanced, Deep, Creative, Code review) work at once on whatever model you use. No model is preconfigured.
- **Code map:** a compact map of the project a conversation works in, so the assistant looks things up instead of reading whole files. Plus four "reverse engineer" skills. Nothing to install.
- **Privacy:** switches off the app's usage reporting and the upload of a conversation when you rate an answer. `/privacy` shows the state.
- **Usage counter:** counts requests and tokens per day and model (never your text).
- **Deep research** and **Code power:** new tools and skills the assistant can use.

Everything else stays switched off until you set it up.

## Changing an add-on's settings

Some add-ons have their own page in **Settings** (Tiers, Modes, Sampling). The rest are set up in the app's settings file. To edit it:

1. Quit DeepSeek Harness.
2. In Finder press **⌘ Shift G**, paste `~/.dsh/profiles/desktop/` and press Return.
3. Make a copy of **`cordis.patch.yml`** first, as your own backup. Then open the original with TextEdit.
4. Paste in the block for the add-on you want, from its section in [docs/ADD-ONS.md](docs/ADD-ONS.md). Fill in the parts in `<ANGLE BRACKETS>`, save, and open the app.

The file is indentation-sensitive: use spaces, never tabs, and keep the lines lined up as in the example. If the app will not start after an edit, put your copy back.

## Updating

Download the newer version and double-click **`Install.command`** again. It replaces the add-ons and keeps your settings.

## Removing

Double-click **`Uninstall.command`**. It removes all twenty-two add-ons and their files. Your conversations and your models are not touched. Any settings you wrote for the add-ons stay in the settings file and do nothing; if you install again, they come back into effect.

## Using it on a second Mac

1. Install the DeepSeek Harness app on the other Mac and open it once.
2. Run **`Install.command`** there too.
3. Add your models in **Settings → Models**.
4. Optional: to keep the same **settings** on both Macs, use iCloud Drive (below).
5. Optional: to see the same **conversations** on both Macs, set up the **Sync** add-on (see [docs/ADD-ONS.md](docs/ADD-ONS.md#sync)). It needs a private git repository that both Macs can reach. Neither Mac has to be switched on for the other to sync.

### Same settings on both Macs, through iCloud Drive

The **Shared settings** add-on keeps the settings you change in the app's own pages in one file, `settings.json`, in a folder in iCloud Drive. 1. On the first Mac, double-click **`Install.command`** and answer **y** when it asks *"Share settings through iCloud Drive?"*. It uses the folder **iCloud Drive → DeepSeek Harness Plus**.

Send them the link to this project, https://github.com/BLCKHWK60/DS-Harness-Plus. They follow **Install** above. Nothing in here contains your addresses, keys or personal settings; every add-on starts empty.

| --- | --- |

| `addons/` | The twenty-two add-ons. Each has a `README.md` with its full technical notes. |
