# dsh-ai-terminal-pet

A DeepSeek Harness (DSH) Cordis bundle that mirrors Harness session state onto
the [AI Terminal Pet](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet) desktop
overlay: a small always-on-top Win32 pet that shows which sessions are working,
which one is waiting for your approval, which failed, and which finished.

The package ships the overlay binary and the official reporter protocol module
inside the tarball, so a single market install is enough to get a pet on screen
that follows **this Harness's** sessions. It does not attach to any other
terminal by itself: sessions from OpenCode, Claude Code and Antigravity appear
only after that terminal's own reporter is installed into it. The repository
README section [Connect your terminal](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet#connect-your-terminal)
has one hook per terminal; the panel, the pipe and the protocol are shared, so
once a terminal reports it shows up next to the Harness sessions.

No npm dependencies, no install scripts, no network calls at runtime (unless the
maintainer pins a release in lib/release-pins.json, see below).

## What it does

| Harness signal | Overlay state |
| --- | --- |
| `turn/start`, `agent/inbox/claimed`, `agent/status` running | working |
| `tool/call` | tool_use |
| `approval/request` (waterfall listener) | waiting_permission |
| `tool/result` with `error`, `agent/error` | error |
| `turn/end`, `agent/status` idle | idle |
| Harness process exit | closed |

Events this table does not list are not part of the Harness session log: there is
no `command/done` or `working-directory/change` in `SessionEventMap`. The project
path, the parent session and the session start time do not come from events at
all - they are read from `session.header` (`cwd`, `parentSession`, `createdAt`),
which is the only place the host states them. That is also why a session shows
the right project even though the desktop Harness itself runs from its install
directory, and why a subagent conversation is nested under the session it was
forked from.

The overlay then plays an alert tone, shows a tray balloon on those transitions
and its one-click jump button targets the Harness window. Plugin reload (HMR)
disposes the listeners but deliberately does not close sessions: only a real
process exit means the conversation is over.

## Where it is listed, and what each market indexes

Three independent paths exist today, and each one reads a different field:

| Market | What it indexes | What this package offers it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| npm registry | package name, version, `dist.integrity` | published as `dsh-ai-terminal-pet`; a market that installs by name gets a verified tarball |
| dshmarket (the market tab most Harness Desktop users run) | `https://awesome-dsh-plugin.com/plugins.json`, which is generated from the [awesome-dsh-plugin](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin) repository | entry merged via PR [#13937](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/13937); the `install` command it renders comes from that entry's pinned `tarball`, so bumping it is always a pull request *there*, never an edit here |
| GitHub-harvesting markets | repositories carrying the `dsh-plugin` topic plus a root `package.json` declaring `name` and `dsh.bundle` | this repository has the topic and the root shim manifest, which is what makes `dsh plugin add github:owner/repo` resolve instead of mounting a 0.0.0 dependency |

"Listed" and "visible" are different states, and only the second one helps a
user: the awesome entry existed before its `plugins.json` entry did, because the
site builds the catalog on a schedule. Check the market's own public index, not
the merged pull request. The package README cannot promise what another
repository's build will render; it can only promise that the fields those builds
read are present and correct.

The package describes itself to storefronts through `dsh.catalog`: a category, a
one-line summary in both languages, and the capabilities it uses. Capabilities
are self-declared and never checked — DSH does not sandbox plugins — so read them
as a description, not a permission grant.
The bundle is Windows only and declares `dsh.bundle.platforms: ["win32"]`, so
other platforms show it as unsupported instead of installing it.

It also declares `dsh.marketplace` (`profiles: ["desktop", "headless", "web"]`,
`requiresBuildApproval: false`, `manualSteps: false`). DSH itself never reads
that field - the bundle mounts through `dsh.bundle` either way - but storefronts
that sort entries by profile do: without it a registry falls back to a
headless-or-web guess and a desktop client hides the entry.

Manually, from a terminal, into a profile you own — by package name, by release
tarball, or by pinning the release tag. All three are verified end to end:

```sh
# by package name: published on npm, no clone, no Go toolchain
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add dsh-ai-terminal-pet

# release tarball: same bytes as the npm release, straight from the GitHub Release
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/download/dsh-plugin-v1.2.8/dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.8.tgz

# git source, pinned to the release tag
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add "git+https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet.git#dsh-plugin-v1.2.8&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet"
```

Those three differ only in transport. The npm path is the shortest and the one a
market uses when it installs by name; the tarball path works when a market pins a
release asset instead of a registry entry; the git path is the fallback for a
machine that cannot reach npm at all. Every one of them lands the same
prebuilt overlay in `vendor/`.

Do not hand pnpm a bare repository URL. pnpm resolves a git dependency by
running the package's lifecycle scripts, and it blocks those for unpinned
git sources until you copy the `allowBuilds` key it prints into your profile's
`pnpm-workspace.yaml`; the failure message never mentions AI Terminal Pet. The
package therefore ships no lifecycle hook, and its vendored overlay is a
committed file rather than a build product. `vendor/manifest.json` records the
SHA-256 of that file, the SHA-256 of the Go sources it was built from, and the
Go version that produced it, so a stale or hand-edited vendor directory fails a
check instead of shipping quietly.

The GitHub and npm paths above need nothing from this repository at install time.
`dsh plugin add dsh-ai-terminal-pet` resolves through the npm registry; the
tarball and git forms resolve through GitHub. A marketplace that indexes npm
sees the package under its own name and can verify the published integrity
digest; a marketplace that indexes repositories sees the `dsh-plugin` topic and
the root shim manifest.

`add` is the whole install: the profile records the dependency, and the bundle
declares itself through `dsh.bundle.patch`, so no separate `enable` step exists.
The profile you add it to has to be the one Harness boots.

Two profiles are special. The reserved `desktop` profile is rejected by the
standalone `dsh` CLI (`profile "desktop" is managed exclusively by the Electron
application`); the Desktop app's own bundled CLI does accept it, and the in-app
plugin manager is the supported path there. Any other profile name is yours.

If the app reports restart-required after enabling the bundle, restart Harness.

## What it writes on disk

First use in a Harness process copies two files, and only when they are missing:

| File | Origin | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| %LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\protocol.js | vendor/protocol.js | pipe name, state set, redaction, snapshot |
| %LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe | vendor/AI-Terminal-Pet.exe | the Win32 overlay |

Nothing is ever overwritten: an existing file, including one placed by the
standalone installer, wins. Set DSH_PET_NO_BOOTSTRAP=1 to skip this step
entirely (for example when the overlay is managed by `scripts/install.ps1` already).

Reports also write the overlay's normal runtime snapshot under the same
directory, exactly like every other reporter.

### Optional download fallback

lib/release-pins.json is absent from the published package by default. When the
maintainer fills it in with pinned release asset URLs, sizes and SHA-256
digests, a machine that has no vendored binary downloads the two assets over
HTTPS with a 30 s timeout, verifies size and digest with node:crypto, and only
then installs them. Any failure is silent apart from one warning; the plugin
keeps working without an overlay.

## The overlay itself is still standalone

This bundle is a convenience. The overlay is a Go application that installs
normally with `scripts/install.ps1` from the repository, and every other reporter
(Claude Code, OpenCode, Antigravity, generic) talks to the same named pipe.
Those reporters are separate installs, not part of this package: a terminal that
has none of them hooked reports nothing, in this install or in any other. A
machine that only wants the overlay does not need this package; a machine that
only wants the plugin gets one installed automatically.

## Requirements and limits

- Windows only (named pipes plus a Win32 layered window).
- Node 22.19+ or 24+ in the Harness runtime.
- Nothing in this package can fail the host: every entry point is wrapped,
  every report is fire-and-forget, and there is no process.exit.
- Session id is the Harness session.header.id; pid is a synthetic per-session
  id and parentPid is the real Harness process, which is how the overlay ties a
  session to its terminal window.

# ai-terminal-pet

Stop glancing across terminal windows to track agent states. It costs one small executable with no account and no cloud.

![ai-terminal-pet](docs/assets/hero.png)

![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows-blue) ![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/go-1.23-00ADD8) ![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-1.0.2-blue)
![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green) ![Size](https://img.shields.io/badge/size-4.17%20MiB-blue) ![Dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/dependencies-3-informational) ![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-206-brightgreen) ![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/dsh-ai-terminal-pet?label=dsh%20plugin)

> 🇬🇧 [English](#english)  ·  🇨🇳 [中文](#中文)

---

## English

### The problem

You run Claude Code, OpenCode, or Antigravity in multiple terminal windows at once. A background task prompts for permission to execute a tool, but you are focused in another window and never notice the prompt.

Fourteen minutes later, you switch back only to discover that your build has been sitting idle the entire time. Glancing across multiple terminal tabs wastes focus and breaks your concentration.

ai-terminal-pet anchors a 56px strip to the screen edge. It aggregates your sessions in real time, pulses when an agent needs permission, and displays which project is waiting and for how long.

The table below contrasts the everyday workflow before and after using the overlay:

| Context | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple terminals | Four terminal windows open; you lose track of which window needs attention. | One 56px strip on the edge of the screen aggregates every active session. |
| Blocked build | You find out a build was blocked on a permission prompt fourteen minutes ago. | The overlay pulses immediately and shows which project is waiting and for how long. |
| Context switching | You click across tabs to check whether builds and tasks are still running. | A single glance reveals current states without touching your keyboard or mouse. |

### What it looks like

![Demo](docs/assets/demo.gif)
*The actual sequence: a session blocks on a permission prompt and the strip breathes, hovering unfolds the session list, and clicking the waiting row brings that terminal forward. Frames are rasterized from the shipped renderer; the ring stands in for the click, since a layered window draws no cursor.*

![Compact strip](docs/assets/overlay-compact.png)
*Compact strip: pulsing state orb with status glyph, session count, state word, and waiting project name.*

![Expanded list](docs/assets/overlay-expanded.png)
*Expanded list: active sessions showing per-row project name, state, source hook, and relative time.*

![Many sessions](docs/assets/overlay-expanded-many.png)
*Expanded list with many sessions: six session rows followed by the overflow line showing remaining sessions.*

![Auto-approve countdown](docs/assets/overlay-auto-approve.png)
*Auto-approve countdown: draining bar with "Allow (5s)" prompt allowing manual veto before automatic permission approval.*

![In context](docs/assets/desktop-scene.png)
*In context: the strip sits at the screen edge beside two terminals, so a blocked session is visible without switching windows. The panel is the real renderer output; the two terminals around it are drawn, since a real capture would contain somebody's project names.*

---

### Features

The table below outlines the core capabilities and exact runtime parameters of the application:

| Feature | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| State aggregation | Aggregates sessions across 7 states (`idle`, `thinking`, `working`, `tool_use`, `waiting_permission`, `error`, `closed`), showing the highest-priority state across all active sessions. |
| Compact and expanded panels | Compact panel occupies 56x156 logical pixels anchored to a screen edge; clicking expands to 200 px wide, displaying 1–6 rows before adding an overflow line. |
| Whole-panel gestures | Click anywhere toggles compact and expanded views, drag anywhere moves 1:1 with the cursor, and mouse wheel adjusts zoom between 65% and 160%. |
| Edge retract | Slides mostly off-screen when docked at an edge leaving a thin sliver; hovering restores it, while waiting_permission or error states override retraction to remain visible. |
| Tray menu | Right-click tray menu toggles visibility, resets position and zoom, opens settings, switches language, toggles autostart, and configures auto-approve. |
| Settings window | Native three-tab window (General, Sound, Sessions) where every change persists immediately to `config.json` without an OK button. |
| Synthesized alert tones | Generates 44.1 kHz 16-bit mono PCM WAV tones in memory across four sound schemes (`chime`, `bell`, `soft`, `pulse`), with separate gates for waiting, error, and finish. |
| Per-session alerts | Fires Windows tray notification balloons and audio alerts on transitions into `waiting_permission`, `error`, or finish states. |
| Auto-approve and denylist | Provides a 5-second veto window on permission prompts where a tap denies and silence approves; blocks commands matching the dangerous-command denylist. |
| Jump to terminal | Walks session process ancestry and matches window titles to bring the waiting terminal window or tab to the foreground. |
| Scriptable CLI | Outputs structured session state via `ai-terminal-pet --json` by reading disk snapshots, avoiding blocking on GUI processes. |
| Single instance | A named mutex makes a second launch activate the running overlay instead of starting another one. |
| Connection capacity | The pipe server accepts 32 concurrent connections with a 5 s read timeout, so IPC never blocks the UI thread. |
| Idle lifecycle | A session is dropped only after a 2-minute absence grace; with no session left, the process removes itself after 10 minutes. |

### How it works

```text
Host CLI (Claude Code / OpenCode / Antigravity)
       │
       ▼ (Fire-and-forget hooks)
reporters/*.js
       │
       ▼ (JSON line over Windows named pipe: \\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>)
AI-Terminal-Pet.exe (Go 1.23, single-instance mutex)
       │
       ├─► internal/pipeserver (32 connections, 5s timeout, OK/ERR response)
       ├─► internal/store (in-memory state, TTL, disk snapshots fallback)
       └─► internal/ui (Win32 layered window, GDI topmost canvas)
```

- **Per-user named pipe**: IPC flows through `\\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>`, where `<8hex>` is derived from the SHA-256 hash of the user home directory. The exact same pipe-name algorithm is implemented in Go and JavaScript, locked by a cross-language golden test.

- **JSON line protocol**: Sessions transmit one JSON line per message with a 1 MiB payload cap. The server replies with an exact `OK` or `ERR` acknowledgment, and reporters retry until a deadline without treating partial reads as success.

- **On-disk snapshots**: Snapshot files under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\runtime\` provide a fallback channel and serve as the authoritative on-disk record of active sessions.

- **OS observation over heartbeats**: Session existence is decided by operating system observation of the process table and window titles rather than reporter heartbeats. A session remains active as long as its terminal window exists, and removal requires the host to be unobservable for a continuous 2-minute grace period.

- **Disks beat heartbeats**: The disk snapshot is authoritative for session existence: a session that was on disk and is gone is over, while synthetic PIDs from hooks never participate in liveness probing.

- **Connection handling**: The server accommodates 32 concurrent connections with a 5s read timeout, keeping IPC processing off the UI thread.

- **GDI rendering**: A top-down 32bpp DIB section created with CreateDIBSection is painted through a memory DC and handed to the layered window with UpdateLayeredWindow.

### Install

There are three ways in. Pick the one that matches how you got here.

**A. DeepSeek Harness user — no Go toolchain, nothing to build**

```powershell
dsh plugin add dsh-ai-terminal-pet
```

The package carries a prebuilt overlay and this project's own `protocol.js`. On first load it copies them into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\` **only when they are missing**, so it never overwrites an install you maintain yourself. That is the whole setup: the panel appears on the next session. It is also on npm as [`dsh-ai-terminal-pet`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-ai-terminal-pet) (1.2.8), and the release tarball, a tag-pinned git source and a bare repository URL all work (`dsh plugin add <path-or-git-url>`); the same bootstrap runs either way.

**B. Everyone else — download a package, no Go toolchain**

Two packages are published for this release: a self-extracting `pet-setup.exe` and a portable zip. Both install the same 11 artifacts into the same directory; the zip additionally lets you look inside before running anything.

1. Download one of them from the [`pet-v1.0.2` release](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/tag/pet-v1.0.2):
   - **`pet-setup.exe`** (13.5 MB): double-click it. It verifies its own payload against `SHA256SUMS.txt` **before** writing anything, then runs the installer inside itself. `pet-setup.exe --verify` re-checks the installed files at any time, `--uninstall` removes them, `--add-to-path` puts the commands on your PATH.
   - **`ai-terminal-pet-1.0.2-win-x64.zip`** (4.99 MB, 17 files): unzip it anywhere and double-click `install.cmd`. Everything is inspectable first; `install.cmd -VerifyOnly`, `-Uninstall` and `-AddToPath` work as they do in the source tree.
2. Verify that the installation works:
   ```powershell
   & "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json
   ```

The zip and the setup exe carry the three binaries, `protocol.js`, the Harness bundle, the installer and a `SHA256SUMS.txt`, so the only thing on Windows is one download and one double-click. Neither needs Go, Node, or an installer framework. The release is **not code-signed yet**, so the first run shows SmartScreen's "unknown publisher" prompt:

![SmartScreen on an unsigned build](docs/assets/smartscreen-unsigned.png)
*What an unsigned build produces on a machine that has never seen it: click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. This image is a reconstruction of the documented dialog, not a capture - see [docs/assets/README.md](docs/assets/README.md).*

That prompt is a certificate the project does not have, not a problem with the file you downloaded — the per-file SHA256 values in `SHA256SUMS.txt` are the honest substitute until a certificate exists.

After installing, `--doctor` should look like this (paths shortened here, everything else is the program's own output):

![--doctor on a healthy install](docs/assets/doctor-green.png)
*Nine checks, and the one that matters when you see an empty panel is `instance` — if it says a live instance is listening, the overlay is healthy and the missing piece is the terminal's reporter, not the install.*

**C. Developers — build from source (Go 1.23+)**

```powershell
# 1. Build the overlay, the native statusline shim and the native hook
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe ./cmd/ai-terminal-pet
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\pet-statusline.exe ./cmd/pet-statusline
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\pet-hook.exe ./cmd/pet-hook

# 2. Install (stops a running overlay, copies, re-hashes every artifact)
.\scripts\install.cmd

# 3. See it work
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json
```

Re-verify the installed artifacts at any time with per-file SHA256 checks:

```powershell
.\scripts\install.cmd -VerifyOnly
```

It prints `install: verified - 11 file(s) match the repository, 0 warning(s)` and exits 0 only when every deployed artifact matches (the 11 artifacts are the overlay, the statusline shim, the native hook `pet-hook.exe`, `protocol.js`, and the 7 files of the DeepSeek Harness bundle). The installer itself stops a running overlay first and waits for the process to release its file handles; a plain file copy over a live binary fails at random, which is what the retry loop and the SHA256 comparison after every copy are for.

`install.cmd` is the entry point rather than `install.ps1` because a stock Windows install runs PowerShell at `RemoteSigned`, and `RemoteSigned` refuses a local `.ps1` that still carries the "downloaded from the internet" zone marker — the exact shape of a file you unzip from a release. The wrapper starts one `powershell.exe` with `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass`, changes no machine or user policy, forwards every argument and every exit code, and adds no install logic: `install.ps1` remains the only implementation, and `.\scripts\install.ps1 -VerifyOnly` works unchanged on a machine whose policy already allows it.

Put `ai-terminal-pet` on your PATH so you can type the bare command:

```powershell
.\scripts\install.cmd -AddToPath
```

It writes **only** `HKCU\Environment\Path` (never `HKLM`), backs the previous value up to `<install dir>\path-backup.txt` first, and does nothing if the directory is already listed. **Open a new terminal** for the change to take effect. `-Uninstall` also removes that PATH entry, so uninstalling does not leave a dead entry behind (the previous value is backed up again, this time into `%TEMP%`).
Without this step the installer does not touch your PATH at all, so keep using the full path `& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json`.

The installer lives under `scripts/` rather than at the repository root on purpose: market indexers fetch a root `install.ps1` by name and regex-scan it, and this script legitimately mentions the `HKCU` Run key and a `-Recurse -Force` cleanup. Moving it one level down takes those two false positives off the root without taking any behaviour off the script.

Run `ai-terminal-pet --doctor` at any point after installing to self-check the environment, install files, runtime state, pipe, autostart entry, and node availability. To remove the deployed artifacts, run `.\scripts\install.cmd -Uninstall`; it asks for a typed `yes` confirmation first, refuses unsafe target directories, and accepts `-Force` for unattended removal.

Installing a terminal hook is required for that terminal to report; see the next section to connect your tools.

### Connect your terminal

| Terminal | How to connect | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| OpenCode | Add `file:///C:/path/to/ai-terminal-pet/reporters/opencode.js` to `plugin` in `opencode.json` | Automatic session tracking for tool use, prompt handling, and task completion |
| Claude Code | Add `& "%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\pet-hook.exe" --mode=claude` for `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, and `Notification` in `settings.json`. `node <repo>/reporters/claude-hook.js` still works and is the fallback when you cannot run the `.exe`. | Real-time status updates, tool execution tracking, and permission prompt alerts |
| Antigravity | Set `statusLine.command` to `pet-statusline.exe` and configure `pet-hook.exe --mode=antigravity` for agent and tool events (`antigravity-hook.js` is the fallback) | Fast statusline updates, agent state changes, and permission request forwarding |
| DeepSeek Harness | Install the Cordis bundle from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\bundles\ai-terminal-pet-bridge\` via the plugin manager (`install_bundle`) | turn/start to working, tool/call to tool_use, approval/asked to waiting_permission, tool/result with an error to error, turn/end to idle, process exit to closed |
| Anything else | Run `node reporters/generic.js` with `--source`, `--state`, and `--project` flags | Instant status reporting from any custom script or CLI tool |

Writing your own reporter for a tool that is not listed here needs no source reading: [docs/PROTOCOL.md](docs/PROTOCOL.md) specifies the wire protocol (fields, state semantics, pipe-name derivation, acknowledgment contract, and redaction rules) that a conforming reporter must implement.

The Harness side is a host-only Cordis bundle: it holds no pipe-name, state-set or snapshot logic of its own, it loads the protocol from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\protocol.js` and delegates everything to it.

The Harness side has a second, self-contained option since `dsh-ai-terminal-pet` `1.1.0`: a standalone DSH plugin package at [`packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet`](packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet), also shipped as a GitHub Release asset. The package is now **1.2.8** (tag `dsh-plugin-v1.2.8`, asset `dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.8.tgz`); 1.2.7, 1.2.6, 1.2.5, 1.2.4, 1.2.3, 1.2.2, 1.2.1, 1.2.0 and 1.1.0 stay published and immutable but are superseded. 1.2.7 shipped the 1.0.1 overlay, whose compact strip answers "which terminal is blocked, and for how long" without expanding the panel; 1.2.8 ships 1.0.2, where the look itself is a setting - three named palettes, an optional per-terminal tint on each row's source name, and "start hidden". 1.2.5 is the first version that works on a machine that never ran the overlay: it declares `vendor/package.json` as CommonJS (without it, `require()` of the shipped protocol returned a namespace with no `sendStatus`, so a `DSH_PET_NO_BOOTSTRAP=1` install silently reported nothing), it reads the project path, lineage and start time from the session header instead of `process.cwd()` (the desktop Harness starts from the install directory, so every session was attributed to one wrong path), and its de-duplication signature now covers state, reason, tool, project, title and parent session instead of state alone. 1.2.4 was a wording fix (one market install read as if it covered every terminal, and it does not - the bundle mirrors **Harness** sessions out of the box, while OpenCode, Claude Code and Antigravity sessions appear only after each of those terminals gets its own reporter); 1.2.3 added the `dsh.marketplace` block a third-party storefront reads before offering a plugin to its desktop client, and 1.2.2 moved the installer from the repository root into `scripts/`, which edits Go comments, which changes the source digest `vendor/manifest.json` records. Release assets cannot be edited, so a wording or manifest fix costs a version - shipping different bytes under an unchanged version is exactly the drift this repository removes. The three install forms are verified end to end, and the 1.2.4 assets were installed again from three fresh directories after the release went out: the release tarball in **1.8 s**, the tag-pinned git source in **3.7 s**, and the repository URL in **6.5 s**, all rc=0, with the unpacked bytes matching `git show ff7f6de:` file for file (a bare `add dsh-ai-terminal-pet` still waits on the npm release described below):

```powershell
# from the release tarball: no git clone, no build step
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/download/dsh-plugin-v1.2.8/dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.8.tgz

# from git, pinned to the release tag
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add "git+https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet.git#dsh-plugin-v1.2.8&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet"

# from the repository URL: resolves through the root manifest shim
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add github:jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet
```

The repository URL works because the repository root now carries a 68-line `package.json` shim that contains no code: it points `main` at the package, declares `dsh.bundle.patch` as `./packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet/cordis.patch.yml` and limits `files` to that subtree. Without it a host that reads the repository root sees no `dsh.bundle`, installs an empty package and warns `declares no dsh.bundle`. The shim is `private`, so it never occupies the npm name, its `version` tracks the package (`verify.mjs` asserts they are equal, so a bump cannot land in one manifest only), and it carries the same `dsh.catalog` block the package does.

The package ships no lifecycle hooks at all — `prepack` was removed in 1.1.0 — because pnpm runs them for a git dependency and fails an unpinned source with an `allowBuilds` error that never mentions AI Terminal Pet. `vendor/` is committed instead and only verified: `node sc

# dsh-remedy (plugin)

The resident half. It mounts at `llm/stream`, repairs a proven fusion, and says
nothing when there is nothing to repair.

## Mount

`cordis.patch.yml` adds one row through `insert:`:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: remedy-stream
      name: dsh-remedy
      config:
        repair: true
        retryOnMalformed: 0
        maxCalls: 8
```

`dsh-remedy` must be the **bare** package specifier: the loader resolves
`dist/index.js` from it.

## Config

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `repair` | `true` | Wrap `llm/stream` |
| `retryOnMalformed` | `0` | Retries per step after `MALFORMED_RESPONSE`; a stop-gap, not the fix |
| `maxCalls` | `8` | Ceiling on calls synthesized from one fused block |
| `journalPath` | unset | Append redacted repair events as JSONL; no writes when unset |
| `log` | `true` | One mount line through `ctx.logger` |

## CLI

```
dsh-remedy status  [--json] [--journal <file>]
dsh-remedy repair  [<file>] [--name <tool>] [--id <call-id>] [--max-calls <n>] [--truncated] [--json]
dsh-remedy scan    <session.jsonl|directory> [--since <iso>] [--max-files <n>] [--json] [--out <file>]
dsh-remedy verify  [--json]
```

`scan` takes one plain `.jsonl` file, a multi-frame `session.v4.jsonl.zstd` log,
or a directory of them; `--since` drops older events and reports how many it
dropped, `--max-files` caps the walk. It also prints the turn census and the
error codes it counted. `repair` reads stdin when no file is given, and a `.json`
fixture through its `arguments` field.

Exit codes: `0` ok · `1` finding · `2` usage · `3` unavailable.

`scan --out` writes the report and a `.sha256` sidecar. A report that finds
fusion exits `1`, because a dead turn is a finding even when the file is valid.

## What the wrapper emits

On a proven fusion it replaces the terminal error with:

```
block-end(index=0, id=<original>)
block-end(index=<next>, id=<original>#remedy-1)
...
finish{kind:'stop'}
```

Everything else passes through unchanged.

# dsh-remedy

[![CI](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/dsh-remedy/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/dsh-remedy/actions)
[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/dsh-remedy.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-remedy)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
[![Node](https://img.shields.io/badge/node-%3E%3D22.19-brightgreen.svg)](https://nodejs.org)
[![Status](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-verified-blue.svg)](#status)

[中文说明](README.zh-CN.md)

dsh-remedy is a resident repair layer for DeepSeek Harness (DSH). It mounts on `llm/stream`, splits tool-call argument text that a relay glued into one index, and re-throws the original failure whenever it cannot prove the split. It also names the failure classes it refuses to repair, so a dead turn comes with a line explaining it instead of silence.

## What it fixes

When an upstream provider relay packs two tool calls into one index, `@earendil-works/pi-ai` receives `{...}{...}` and throws. `dsh-llm-pi-ai` converts this into `LlmError(..., 'MALFORMED_RESPONSE')`, and `dsh-agent-loop` aborts the turn because `MALFORMED_RESPONSE` is not in `retryableCodes`. Upstream discussion deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness #4427 describes the same failure family.

```text
Tool call "<name>": Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON at position N
Received arguments: {...}{...}
```

Measured over this machine's session directory: 78 session files, 393 attempts, 38 fused calls, 44 `MALFORMED_RESPONSE` failures of which 39 are repairable, and 0 unreadable lines.

The turn census of the same directory counted 293 turns: 94 completed, 88 `max_tokens`, 100 error and 11 aborted. The error codes it named are `MALFORMED_RESPONSE` 44, `UNSUPPORTED_REASONING_EFFORT` 37, `SERVER` 16, `UNKNOWN` 1, `MISSING_CREDENTIAL` 1 and `INVALID_REQUEST` 1.

Two of those classes needed different treatment, and both are now visible:

- `MALFORMED_RESPONSE` is a fusion, so it is repaired when the split can be proven.
- `UNSUPPORTED_REASONING_EFFORT` is a deterministic refusal: a profile asked for a level the adapter does not offer (`provider "opendesign" model "deepseek-v4.1-flash-eco" does not support reasoning effort "xhigh"`). Retrying it spends a request to learn the same answer twice, so the plugin names it once and refuses to touch it.

## Install

Install the plugin into a DSH profile:

```bash
dsh plugin --profile <name> add dsh-remedy
```

Install as a project dependency:

```bash
pnpm add dsh-remedy dsh-remedy-core
```

Version 0.3.0 of the plugin cannot be installed from the registry, because npm published its raw workspace manifest with a literal `workspace:*` dependency. Every release after it ships a pnpm-packed tarball instead. Version 0.3.1 carried the same manifest fix but was superseded before it reached the registry.

Source workflow for contributors:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/dsh-remedy.git
cd dsh-remedy
pnpm install
pnpm run verify
```

## How it works

dsh-remedy buffers incoming tool-call deltas on the `llm/stream` Cordis seam:

```text
Input chunks:
  block-start { id: "call_01", name: "ops_bash" }
  tool-call-delta '{"command":"ls"}{"command":"pwd"}'
  finish { kind: 'error', error: LlmError('MALFORMED_RESPONSE') }

Repaired output:
  block-start { id: "call_01", name: "ops_bash" }
  block-end   { arguments: '{"command":"ls"}' }
  block-start { id: "call_01#remedy-1", name: "ops_bash" }
  block-end   { arguments: '{"command":"pwd"}' }
  finish      { kind: 'stop' }
```

The repair is all-or-nothing. Every open buffer must parse into top-level JSON objects. If all of them are proven, each call gets its own `block-start` and `block-end` and the error finish becomes `{kind:'stop'}`. If any buffer cannot be proven, nothing is emitted and the original failure goes out untouched.

A second listener runs on `agent/request-error`, which the loop calls after a failed attempt:

```text
no code, empty code, or an aborted signal  → next()
UNSUPPORTED_REASONING_EFFORT,              → name it once per step and code, then next()
INVALID_REQUEST, MISSING_CREDENTIAL,
EMPTY_RESPONSE
IMAGE_OFFLOAD_REQUIRED, INVALID_CREDENTIAL → next()
MALFORMED_RESPONSE with budget left        → { kind: 'retry' }
anything else, or budget spent              → next()
```

That order follows the contract the runtime documents: a handling listener returns `{ kind: 'retry' }` **without** calling `next()`, and a listener that does not own the decision must return `next()`. Calling `next()` first and then overriding its answer would discard what the default chain decided, and context compaction authorizes its own retry on exactly that path.

Retry is off by default (`retryOnMalformed: 0`). The budget is a bounded cache of 256 entries per process, which is far more than one turn needs and small enough that a long-lived desktop session cannot grow it.

## Ask it what is happening

`dsh-remedy explain` reads the registry, an optional profile layer and an optional session directory, and prints one row per failure class: how often this machine hit it, which patch covers it, and whether that patch is switched on in the profile you named.

```bash
dsh-remedy explain --sessions ~/.dsh/sessions --profile-file ~/.dsh/profiles/<name>/cordis.patch.yml
```

```text
failure class                turns  covered by          enabled here
---------------------------  -----  -------------------  -------------------
completed                      124  (none)               (none)
max-tokens                      88  by design            no (by design)
MALFORMED_RESPONSE              47  P-0001…P-0005,P-0011 P-0001…P-0005
UNSUPPORTED_REASONING_EFFORT    37  P-0013               P-0013
SERVER                          16  by design            no (by design)
MISSING_CREDENTIAL               1  P-0013               P-0013
```

Without `--sessions` it prints no counts rather than a row of zeros, and without `--profile-file` it says the answer is unknown rather than assuming the default. A class this machine hits, that a patch covers, but that your profile switched off, makes it exit 1.

## Safety guarantees

- Top-level JSON objects are split strictly at depth zero; `}{` inside a JSON string is not a boundary.
- The first split call keeps its original id; synthetic calls receive `<id>#remedy-N`.
- If any buffer cannot be proven, nothing is emitted and the original failure is re-thrown.
- A single object that fails to parse is rejected, never split.
- The plugin mounts only its own rows, adding no route, no tool and no UI.
- The plugin writes nothing to disk unless `journalPath` is configured.
- `retryOnMalformed` defaults to 0 because retry is a stop-gap, not the fix.
- An empty tool name is rejected (`missing-name`) and never dispatched.
- A tool name that changes inside one index aborts the rescue (`name-changed`) and the original failure is re-thrown.
- Adapter `replayState` is preserved across a repaired finish.
- A `block-end` repair is held until the tool-call phase ends; a later rejection in the same stream withdraws it (`rolled-back`) and the original chunks go out.
- `maxCalls` bounds the calls synthesized for the whole stream, not per block.
- A consumer that stops early is recorded as `consumer-abort`, never as quiet.
- A synthesized call is emitted as a `block-start` plus a `block-end`, never a bare `block-end`.
- A withdrawn repair returns its calls to the stream `maxCalls` budget.
- A `max-tokens` stream is counted as truncated, never as an unrepaired fusion.
- A provider error that passes through is counted in `errors`.
- A pure refusal raises `refused` and never `fused`.
- A budget refusal (`too-many-calls`) raises `fused`, `refused` and `unrepaired`, because no repair happened.
- The four verdict words are unchanged (`unmeasured`, `quiet`, `degraded`, `repaired`), evaluated in that order; only the counter line grew, to eight names plus the optional `resealed`.
- A bare member value is quoted only when exactly one segment reproduces the whole text as one plain object with a byte-identical payload.
- Zero candidates is refused as `bare-value-unproven`; two or more is refused as `ambiguous-bare-value` instead of guessed.
- A stream whose only defect was a reseal reads `repaired`, never `quiet`.
- The retry listener names a diagnosis exactly once per step and code, so a host-level retry of the same failure cannot fill the journal with the same sentence.
- A cancellation is never overridden by a retry.
- Control codes (`IMAGE_OFFLOAD_REQUIRED`, `INVALID_CREDENTIAL`, `MISSING_CREDENTIAL`) are passed through and never retried.
- `scan` reads a multi-frame zstd log through `decompressSessionLog`, the same reader the plugin ships.
- A directory scan keeps one auditable row per file.
- `--since` reports what it dropped as `before_since` instead of hiding it.
- An undecompressable file is a failure line and exit 3, never a silent zero.
- Redaction matches a home path escaped with one or two backslashes as well as the session directory that encodes it.
- The scan counts every `turn/end` (completed, `max_tokens`, aborted, error) and names every `reason.error.code`.
- The census is reported and never promoted into a finding, so the exit code still turns on `fused_calls` and `fusion_failures` alone.
- The byte budget is a gate, not a paragraph: it measures the modules a mounted plugin loads (residency), the modules only a command loads, and the total, and every emitted module must belong to exactly one of the first two.

## What it does not do

| Limit | Reality |
|---|---|
| Attribution | Stops at the assembled text: the plugin cannot prove whether the relay or the adapter glued the objects. |
| Truncation | A `max-tokens` cut is missing bytes and is not repaired. |
| Localized messages | The fallback parses the English `Received arguments:` text; a localized host message disables that fallback, though delta buffering still works. |
| Headless session files | A headless profile does not persist `assistant/attempt` streams, so the artifact reports 0 fused calls; the journal counters and the synthetic id carry the proof. |
| Synthetic IDs | `<id>#remedy-N` are traceability aids, not durable identities. |
| Desktop completion | The desktop artifact records `turn_end=aborted` because the operator stopped after the answer. |
| App cache | Verification applies to the recorded tarball's sha256, not to whatever a running app has cached. |
| Verdict granularity | One verdict word cannot express "observed and correctly refused"; only the counter line can. |
| Journal migration | Existing journal lines are not migrated; in a mixed journal `status --json` reports the shape of the last line. |
| Custom index tracking | An adapter that closes blocks itself and keeps its own index bookkeeping is still unmeasured (`BS-11`). |
| Request retries | Off by default. `SERVER`, `TRANSPORT` and `TIMEOUT` are already retried upstream, so this plugin only retries `MALFORMED_RESPONSE`, and only inside a budget you set. |
| Reasoning effort | The plugin can tell you a configured effort will be refused, but it never changes it for you. `agent/pre-step` is deliberately not mounted: nobody has measured what a user sees when a plugin rejects a step. |
| Mid-stream withdrawal | Measured unreachable on this host: none of the persisted attempt streams carried a provable fusion inside a `block-end`, which is what `rolled-back` requires (`BS-14`). |

## Verify it yourself

```bash
dsh-remedy verify
dsh-remedy scan ~/.dsh/sessions --json
dsh-remedy explain --sessions ~/.dsh/sessions
pnpm run verify
node scripts/gate.mjs --mutate
```

Every artifact in `data/results/` is script-produced and has a `.sha256` sidecar. Two are worth opening first: the live run `data/results/live-2026-11-12T12-20-00.000Z.json` and the corpus replay `data/results/malformed-replay-2026-11-12T11-30-00.000Z.json`.

The whole `MALFORMED_RESPONSE` corpus on one machine was replayed through the built engine: 47 turns, 39 repaired, 8 refused, and no repaired case dispatched a call whose arguments failed to parse. A generated stress pass of 300000 argument texts asserts the same invariant with a recorded seed.

## Status

P-0001, P-0002 and P-0003 are `verified` on a real host: P-0001 on a headless profile and on the desktop app, P-0002 on a 2026-11-10 headless run that repaired a real two-call fusion and saw the synthesized call dispatched, and P-0003 on a 2026-11-10 headless run whose journal wrote a non-zero `refused` after the code declined to repair a budget refusal.

P-0004, P-0005, P-0006, P-0007, P-0008, P-0009, P-0010, P-0011, P-0012 and P-0013 are `tested`, not `verified`. Each has unit tests and negative controls, and a measured fixture, scan or corpus where one exists. P-0004, P-0006 and P-0009 change an offline reader; P-0005 has no live bare-value shape yet; P-0007 and P-0012 are build-side; P-0010 changes the CLI usage text; and P-0011 and P-0013 sit on a seam a live journal witnesses only when a turn fails in a class this plugin retries, which the default budget of 0 never triggers.

Release status: `0.3.8` is published and is the registry `latest` for both `dsh-remedy` and `dsh-remedy-core`. The previous release is `0.3.7`.

Package sizes:

- 0.3.8 plugin: 35898 bytes compressed, 35 files, 117750 bytes unpacked (81740 bytes of `dist/*.js`, 26605 bytes of `dist/*.d.ts`, 3583 bytes of `fixtures/`, 5822 bytes of package-root files), shasum `3bc47df12f21fe7d68336f595d397ff868b3d4d7`.
- 0.3.8 core: 26551 bytes compressed, 21 files, 83461 bytes unpacked (58062 bytes of `dist/*.js`, 22102 bytes of `dist/*.d.ts`), shasum `0df993f85589e101b15b830fa105e7ef8c66c5d5`.
- 0.3.7 plugin: 29462 bytes compressed, 29 files, 98001 bytes unpacked, shasum `69087301f5ff802e387061af61756b65b883b11d`; core: 20000 bytes compressed, 19 files, 65961 bytes unpacked, shasum `33eaaf0320eb474d5d7c5ce2761f10de79d17d21`.
- No sourcemaps are shipped; that removal is worth 41926 bytes of unpacked payload.

The emitted plugin budget is three checks: residency 41075 of 44000 bytes (the modules a mounted plugin loads), cli 40665 of 42000 bytes (the modules only a command loads), and a total of 81740 of 83000 bytes. Per-file caps: `repair-stream.js` 28000, `session-scan.js` 14000, `cli.js` 12000. A patch that crosses a per-file number splits that file instead of absorbing it.

## Development

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm run verify
pnpm run gate
node scripts/gate.mjs --mutate
```

Six gates run on every change: `ssot`, `registry`, `namespace`, `step-review`, `copy`, `size`. `--mutate` breaks each one on purpose and requires every one to go red; it currently catches 6 of 6. The suite is 228 tests and 0 failing.

## Contributing

- Issues and pull requests are welcome.
- A behaviour change needs a failing test first.
- `pnpm run verify` must pass, and `node scripts/gate.mjs --mutate` must catch every gate.
- Gates use Node built-ins only; a new gate must be registered in `audit/gate_ledger.json`.
- No new runtime dependency in `dsh-remedy-core`.
- A patch cannot claim `verified` without a `data/results/live-*` artifact.
- Outward text is checked, not authored freely: every number in it must exist in `docs/copy/facts/public-repo-facts.md`, and the bytes must match `docs/copy/manifest.json`.

## Security

Security reports should use GitHub private vulnerability reporting on the public repository: https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/dsh-remedy/security/policy

## License

MIT. Independent project; not affiliated with DeepSeek.

evidence.readmeExcerpt: # dsh-moonstyle 给 **DeepSeek Harness（DSH）** 用的月光主题：冷白偏蓝的浅色、深海军蓝的深色、圆润字体，强调色一个都不改。除了配色，还顺手把侧栏按 ds-bot 的样子减负——空白的左上角、贴边的小齿轮、能调的标题长度、能关掉的时间戳、上下键切会话。 > 为「性能敏感」而做。常见的主题插件会叠壁纸层、毛玻璃、挂 DOM 观察器，持续吃 GPU 和电；这个插件反过来：**重算一张样式表就完事，运行时没有定时器、没有观察器、没有 `backdrop-filter`。** *配色渲染示意，不是应用截图。上排气泡形态、下排会话形态；左列浅色、右列深色。* --- ## 功能 设置 → 通用 →「主题细节」，七个控件全部实时生效。 | 控件 | 选项 | 作用 | |---|---|---| | **消息形态** | 气泡 / 会话 | 助手回复套不套圆角面板（你的消息始终是靛蓝底白字） | | **配色** | 月光 / 原生 | 切换到 DSH 原厂色板，随时对比 | | **侧栏装饰** | 显示 / 精简 | 精简 = 左上角整块清空、左下角头像换成贴边齿轮 | | **正文字重** | 0–100 无级 | 正文笔画厚薄，只加墨，不改字号与排版 | | **侧栏字重** | 0–100 无级 | 侧栏文字的笔画厚薄，与正文分开调 | | **侧栏标题长度** | 4–12 字无级 | 会话名显示到第几个字，超出省略号 | | **侧栏时间** | 隐藏（默认）/ 显示 | 空闲行那串「刚刚 / 5分钟」；进行中、待回答等状态始终显示 | 另外三件事不用设置： - **侧栏分两级字号**：分组上方的文件夹/项目名是 16px 半粗，会话名保持 14px 正文字号——一眼能看出哪行是标题、哪行是内容。 - **点侧栏「工作区」两个字 → 已归档会话直接铺开**（再点收起），且自动点掉「展开其余 N 个」把每组撑满。 - **`↑` / `↓` 切换会话**，到顶再按 `↑` 回到最下面、到底再按 `↓` 回到最上面，正文不再跟着方向键滚动。输入框有内容、弹窗/菜单打开、带修饰键时自动交还。 ## 为什么用它 **轻。** 一套主题通常意味着持续的 GPU 开销，这里几乎没有： | 项目 | 数值 | |---|---| | 注入的 `

evidence.readmeExcerpt:
English | Simplified Chinese



Hire Google's Antigravity CLI (`agy`) as a staffer for **Claude Code**, **OpenAI Codex**, **DeepSeek Harness**, **Pi**, and **OpenCode**. [![With lead, the host directs workers; with brain, Carbon / Argon proposes and the host verifies.](assets/design.png)](assets/design.svg) **[Bench](#-bench--harness--orchestration) · [Install](#install) · [Examples](#cujs) · [Core design](#core-design) · [Build your own](#build-one-for-another-cli) · [Upgrade](#upgrade)** ## What & Why agy-staff pairs your senior agents with `agy`, which ships **Gemini 4 Carbon**, **Gemini 4 Argon**, and fast **Gemini 4 Hydrogen**. Two orchestration modes (`lead` and `brain`), five personas (`staffer`, `researcher`, `reviewer` for code **and** plans, `implementer`, `ask`), and a model-facing `jobs` skill. Claude Code uses `/agy:` and Codex uses `$agy:`. GPT-6.1-Sol is slow even with fast mode on; Claude Code is quicker, but Fable quota is too scarce to spend grinding through every survey and review. agy gives you both a **fast worker** and a **second brain**: **Hydrogen** handles quick second opinions, research, reviews, and scoped implementation off to the side, while **Carbon** and **Argon** are strong enough in design and world knowledge to pair with Astra or Fable as a peer orchestrator — proposing routes from a second model family while your host checks assumptions and delivers. ![two overloaded senior agents hand the baton to one fast agy worker](assets/why.png) ## Bench — Harness & Orchestration agy-staff Bench v1 runs Claude Code and Codex on three benchmarks, each task three ways: alone, with their own subagents, and with agy through `lead`. [Tech Report](https://lastwhisper.dev/en/zen-of-harness-engineering/agy-staff-bench-v1/) · [中文报告](https://lastwhisper.dev/zen-of-harness-engineering/agy-staff-bench-v1/) [![agy-staff Bench v1: Claude Code and Codex on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-Atlas QnA and DeepSearchQA, solo, with their own subagents and with agy](bench/results/v1/summary.png)](bench/README.md) > [!NOTE] > **Why a bench.** It runs the same tasks on different hosts, with and without agy, to answer three questions: > - **When to delegate.** Which tasks and which hosts gain from handing work to agy, and which are better left solo. The answers become best practices for using agy-staff. > - **What to fix in agy-staff.** Each run shows where delegation wastes time or tokens. Those findings go back into the plugin as fixes, and later bench versions check whether the fixes worked. > - **How harnesses differ.** Same prompt, same worker, different host. Gaps in the results trace back to design choices in each harness. **What v1 says** (one run per task and setup, so a first baseline, not a verdict): - **agy suits research best.** DeepSearchQA is the only benchmark where agy cut host spend on both hosts: Claude Code −39%, Codex −16%. Host spend is what your Claude or ChatGPT plan pays. - **Claude Code's harness suits agy better.** With agy, Claude Code's host spend fell on all three benchmarks (−16% to −39%). Codex's rose on two (SWE-bench +86%, QnA +22%). Claude Code waits in the background until the agy job ends; Codex polls, and every wake-up carries its full context. - **The price is time.** Median time per task rose from 2–8 minutes alone to 13–26 minutes with agy. Tasks solved matched solo or dropped by one. **Method, caveats and versions →** [bench/README.md](bench/README.md) ## How ### Invoke a persona Type `/agy:` in Claude Code and the orchestration modes and personas are right there: ![the /agy: command menu in Claude Code](assets/claude-code-screenshot.png) Same plugin in Codex, invoked with `$agy`: ![the $agy skill picker in Codex](assets/codex-desktop-screenshot.png) In DeepSeek Harness, with the visual `agy staff` subagent sidebar and `/agy-*` role cards: ![the agy staff visual subagent sidebar in DeepSeek Harness](assets/deepseek-harness-screenshot.png) ### Install #### For humans Step 1 — install the Antigravity CLI ([official docs](https://antigravity.google/docs/cli/install)), then verify with `agy --version`. Node.js is also required: ```bash curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash ``` Step 2 — install the plugin into your harness: ```bash claude plugin marketplace add keli-wen/agy-staff claude plugin install agy@agy-staff ``` ```bash codex plugin marketplace add https://github.com/keli-wen/agy-staff codex plugin add agy@agy-staff ```
Using DeepSeek Harness? Install in the **DeepSeek Harness** desktop app (**Plugins** in the left sidebar → install from package spec `github:keli-wen/agy-staff`), or from the terminal: ```bash dsh plugin --profile desktop add github:keli-wen/agy-staff ``` For a local checkout during development, run `dsh plugin --profile desktop add /absolute/path/to/agy-staff` (use `--profile web` if running the web profile). `pnpm`, Node.js, and an authenticated `agy` on `PATH` are required. Once enabled, the plugin mounts the **`agy staff`** visual subagent right-sidebar, native Cordis tools (`agy_brain`, `agy_worker`, `agy_job`), and all eight `/agy-*` skills (`/agy-brain`, `/agy-lead`, `/agy-staffer`, `/agy-researcher`, `/agy-reviewer`, `/agy-implementer`, `/agy-ask`, `/agy-jobs`). Upgrade with `dsh plugin --profile desktop add 'github:keli-wen/agy-staff#'`.
Using Pi? Install: `pi install git:github.com/keli-wen/agy-staff`. Skills are prefixed as `/skill:agy-` (e.g. `/skill:agy-ask reply with OK`), including `/skill:agy-lead`, `/skill:agy-brain`, and `/skill:agy-jobs` for job management. Update with `pi update --extension git:github.com/keli-wen/agy-staff`, then run `/reload`.
Using OpenCode? With OpenCode V1 (verified on 1.18.34), install the package through its native plugin manager: ```bash opencode plugin 'agy-staff@git+https://github.com/keli-wen/agy-staff.git' --global ``` Restart OpenCode, then run `/agy-ask reply with OK`. The plugin automatically registers all eight `agy-*` skills and their native slash commands, including `/agy-lead`, `/agy-brain`, and `/agy-jobs`. No separate skills path or command wrappers are needed. Node.js and an authenticated `agy` are required, as above. OpenCode caches the complete package spec. Restarting does not refresh an unchanged Git spec. To upgrade, choose a newer Git tag or commit and run `opencode plugin 'agy-staff@git+https://github.com/keli-wen/agy-staff.git#' --global --force`, then restart. See [the reference](docs/REFERENCE.md#opencode) for config and local development. OpenCode V2 is not covered by this adapter.
Restart Claude Code or Codex afterwards. First run: `/agy:ask reply with OK` (Claude Code) or `$agy:ask reply with OK` (Codex). Ask is tool-free and needs no setup. > [!IMPORTANT] > **There is no mandatory setup step.** `staffer`, `researcher`, `reviewer` and `implementer` run **unrestricted** by default: agy can inspect the repo, run commands, and edit files. agy-staff keeps that practical with prompts that adapt to the current repo state. For example, when `implementer` starts in a dirty workspace, the companion tells agy which files already had changes and reminds it not to overwrite or deliver unrelated user work. If the task asks for a commit, push, or PR, agy can do that delivery; otherwise it leaves a working-tree diff for review. These prompt instructions do not provide permission isolation. > `setup` + `--restricted` is **optional hardening** for untrusted input — per run (`--restricted`) or as a per-repo default (`setup --restrict review,research`). `setup` dry-runs and asks before writing anything ("set up agy" triggers it); read the [permission notes](docs/REFERENCE.md#optional-hardening-setup) first — the allowlist is prefix-matched, applies machine-wide, and a restricted run can return less than an unrestricted one. #### For agents Paste this into any coding agent: ``` Read the raw text of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/keli-wen/agy-staff/master/docs/INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md (curl it — do not work from a summary) and follow it to install and verify the agy-staff plugin for the harness you are running in. Respond in the user's language. ``` #### Upgrade Claude Code and Codex install a *copy*, so a new version only reaches you when you pull it in yourself: ```bash claude plugin marketplace update agy-staff && claude plugin update agy@agy-staff ``` ```bash codex plugin marketplace upgrade && codex plugin add agy@agy-staff # then restart Codex ``` Claude Code and Codex cache per version directory, so an upgrade lands only if the plugin version changed; restart the harness afterwards. If a fix does not show up, see [upgrading](docs/REFERENCE.md#upgrading) — it has the force-refresh command. ### CUJs Examples below use Claude Code's `/agy:…`; in Codex use `$agy:…`, in Pi `/skill:agy-…`, and in DeepSeek Harness or OpenCode `/agy-…`. | Use case | Invocation | |---|---| | Lead an ongoing task | `/agy:lead investigate the options, draft a proposal, and revise it with my feedback` | | Ask Carbon / Argon to propose the route | `/agy:brain design a migration; check the assumptions before implementing` | | Quick second opinion | `/agy:ask what's your backend model` | | A general task | `/agy:staffer summarize the open TODOs in this repo` | | Generate an image | `/agy:staffer generate a pixel-art robot mascot, save it as assets/mascot.png` | | Review the working tree | `/agy:reviewer Review the current working tree` | | Review a PR | `/agy:reviewer Review PR #730` | | Review a plan or decision | `/agy:reviewer Challenge the migration plan in docs/plan.md` | | Survey a topic | `/agy:researcher how does auth work in this repo` | | Implement a scoped fix | `/agy:implementer fix the flaky retry test` | | Job ops (wait/status/cancel/continue) | natural language: "is the agy job done?", "continue: also check the error path" | `reviewer` is fully prompt-based: you describe the subject and agy gathers the evidence itself (`gh pr view`, `git diff`, reading the file) — there is no flag for handing it a diff. It has two flavors, routed by subject: code review (severity-ranked findings) and general review (a multi-angle challenge of a plan, design, or decision). `staffer` also covers agy's native tools without a dedicated specialist persona, including **image generation** (`generate_image`). A trial on agy v1.1.15 produced a 1024×1024 PNG in about 30 seconds; actual time depends on the task and environment. ## Core design `lead` adds task orchestration guidance for your current agent. Within lead, orient enough to frame the assignment, delegate substantive work to `staffer` by default, wait for the result, then assess it and integrate or follow up. Specialists provide dedicated guidance when useful, while `ask` is reserved for testing. The host owns cross-task decisions, acceptance, integration, and delivery, using the existing jobs workflow. With `brain`, **Carbon** (or **Argon** via `--model argon`) proposes the route first. The host supplies the goal and evidence, challenges assumptions before execution, and owns verification. See the [brain skill](skills/brain/SKILL.md). `ask` answers in the same call. The other personas return a job id and a collection command, such as `wait --timeout 10m`. Your agent waits using the host's available capabilities, with one independent background wait per job where supported. The main agent waits for the final result by default. If you explicitly ask about progress, it can use `observe` to read a snapshot of recent tool activity and response text; it does not query progress for routine updates. Once the task finishes, `wait` or `result` delivers the full report. Expiring a wait leaves the worker running. The timeline below follows a background task from delegation to completion. The host agent waits for the final result by default (or advances already-identified independent work), checks progress when asked, and collects the report. [![A background task over time: the host delegates, waits or observes, while the worker continuously saves AGY output and eventually delivers the full report](assets/integration.png)](assets/integration.svg) Jobs have a separate execution deadline: default 60 minutes, configurable at launch with `--timeout` up to 120 minutes. Use `cancel` to stop execution, or explicitly request `continue` or `restart` after inspecting the existing work. The host harness controls when your agent receives a background result. **Full reference →** [docs/REFERENCE.md](docs/REFERENCE.md) (flags, permission model, jobs/state, troubleshooting, upgrading). **Release notes →** [docs/releases/](docs/releases/). ## Build one for another CLI agy-staff's design is portable: bash plus skills, with no hard dependency on a host, a worker CLI or a runtime library. [docs/DESIGN.md](docs/DESIGN.md) writes it down as best practice. To build the same kind of tool for another agent CLI, give your coding agent this prompt: ``` Read the raw text of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/keli-wen/agy-staff/master/docs/DESIGN.md (curl it — do not work from a summary). Then design an integration that lets this host agent delegate work to the same way. First read ` --help`, map what the CLI supports to the section "What depends on the worker CLI", and list the principles it cannot support before writing any code. Ask me before any call that spends model quota. Respond in the user's language. ``` Before writing any code, the agent lists the principles your CLI cannot support, so you know up front where the tool will degrade. ## Community - [LINUX DO](https://linux.do/) — A next-generation Linux community. ## Contributing Contributions are welcome — issues, bug reports and pull requests all help. A few things worth knowing before you open a PR: - **Run the tests**: `npm test`. The standard suite uses temporary repos and HOME directories with fake `agy`, plus focused module tests. Keep regression tests offline and independent of personal settings. Real AGY validation is a separate opt-in suite described in [tests/README.md](tests/README.md). - **Docs come in pairs**: `README.md` / `README.zh-CN.md` and `docs/REFERENCE.md` / `docs/REFERENCE.zh-CN.md` are kept in sync. Change one, change its counterpart. - **Runtime code lives in `companion/`**: the entrypoint handles modes and job commands; separate modules handle streaming execution, observations and state locking. Skills call the companion, and `templates/` holds the shared prompts. - **Canonical skills are the source of truth**: edit personas in `skills/`, never in `pi-skills/` or `opencode-skills/`. Run `npm run generate:skills` to generate both host entrypoints, and `npm run check:skills` to verify consistency. The existing `generate:pi` and `check:pi` commands remain available. Use `npm run pack:checked` to check freshness before packing; publishing also runs the check. Adding a mode or a flag changes the public surface, so please open an issue first and we can agree on the shape. ## License MIT — see [LICENSE](LICENSE).

decision.reason: Held for versioned DSH compatibility, package or companion artifact mapping. MIT and own Git install are documented. Root exports target OpenCode while its DSH patch references dsh/index.mjs; that fixed file registers native DSH tools and skills and spawns a companion process. The root artifact/export-to-DSH mapping and external authenticated agy runtime are not fully reconciled, and root engines only declare OpenCode, not DSH. prepublishOnly checks generated skills. No candidate code or lifecycle hooks were executed; runtime safety and compatibility are unproven.

# dsh-agent-world > 把多智能体协作搬进一座**可视化 3D 小镇**：每个真实 subagent 是一个会走动的角色， > 每件任务是一张可被拾取的工单，每次调度是一次空间上的移动与协作。 底座沿用 [`@nanmicoder/dsh-agent-teams`](https://github.com/NanmiCoder/dsh-agent-teams) 的语义 （lead 领队 + durable members + 依赖感知任务 + 邮箱 + 调度器）， 但**呈现层从 React 面板换成 three.js 的 3D 场景**。 **状态：R10（内容库层 + 契约层 + 模拟内核 + 运行时 + 2D 俯视面板）。** **3D 场景还没接上**，而且 M4 目前**卡在断网**（装不上 `three`、也搜不了现成场景）—— 完整队列见 [`docs/BACKLOG.md`](docs/BACKLOG.md)，进度台账见 [`docs/PROGRESS.md`](docs/PROGRESS.md)。 设计上它**按游戏的结构组织**：代码是机制，内容是数据。模型库、动作库、任务库、场景库等 **十个内容库**各管一件事，用稳定 id 互相引用，可整包替换 / 升级 / 切换，代码一行不动。 详见 [`docs/CONTENT.md`](docs/CONTENT.md)。 --- ## 现在能干什么 装到 profile 后，模型可以调用四个工具： | 工具 | 副作用 | 说明 | |---|---|---| | `agent_world_open` | **会丢弃当前世界并重建**（当前只在内存） | 按内容包建一座小镇：4 地块 / 10 站点 / 8 角色 | | `agent_world_status` | 无（只读） | 世界摘要 + 花名册 + 工单板 + **内容来源** | | `agent_world_content` | 无（只读） | 装了哪些包、各库多少条、某个 id 的提供方链 | | `agent_world_dispatch` | **会往世界追加工单** | 用**任务库**派一整条工作流进来 | 世界**会自己动**：运行时每 `tickMs`（默认 100ms）推进一步，角色按依赖与工位自己领活、 走过去、干活、完工、把活交接给下一个人（会有**纸条**从一个人飞向另一个人）。 「花名册」长这样： ``` · 工头阿金（lead）待命 @ 广场 · 手头：— · 小蓝（工程师）干活 @ 工位 A · 手头：《改代码》 ``` **现在能看见它**：插件在宿主 HTTP 上挂一个前缀（默认 `/agent-world`）， 里面是 `GET /api/world` 快照、`POST /api/command` 命令，以及一张 **canvas 俯视图**（地块 / 站点 / 角色 / 飞行中的纸条）。 那个俯视图是**永久保留的调试视图**——3D 接上之后仍然有用（决策 D21）。 > ⚠️ **现在还没有真的装进任何 profile**，所以上面这些在你的 GUI 里暂时调不到。 > 本仓库根 `pnpm install` 目前也是坏的（被 `packages/dsh-daily` 的过期 RC 钉死）， > 安装路径**尚未验证过**。 ## 设计（先读这个再读代码） * [`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) —— **架构定稿**。 技术选型（为什么是 three.js 不是 Godot）、三层架构、世界模型、模拟循环的确定性要求、 渲染层分层与性能预算、同步协议、与真实 subagent 的桥、里程碑、决策记录。 * [`docs/CONTENT.md`](docs/CONTENT.md) —— **内容库规范**。十个库各装什么、条目长什么样、 内容包怎么写、三种操作（新增 / 替换 / 切换）、校验规则、一个完整的资产替换示例、常见错误对照表。 * [`docs/PROTOCOL.md`](docs/PROTOCOL.md) —— **模块协议规范**。三层协议（端口 / 线协议 / 边界规则）、 模块边界表、加模块与加消息的步骤、为什么现在不做 protobuf、常见错误对照表。 * [`docs/CONTRACTS.md`](docs/CONTRACTS.md) —— **契约制度**。什么算契约（六要素 + 四件套）、 稳定性分级与版本规则、失败语义总表、48 条契约目录、扩展清单与治理流程。**改任何契约前先读它。** * [`docs/STAGE-ACTIONS.md`](docs/STAGE-ACTIONS.md) —— **舞台动作与反应协议**。状态是基线、 动作是叠加；13 条动作 + 5 条反应的触发/通道/优先级/降级，以及可跑的验收门面。 * [`docs/AGENT-MODEL.md`](docs/AGENT-MODEL.md) —— **Agent 长期模型**。两层身份（人↔身体）、 profile、经验账本与等级派生、专属知识库、任务集与派单；三条跨域纪律与失败降级。 * [`docs/AI-DEBUG.md`](docs/AI-DEBUG.md) —— **AI 调试手册**。`?debug=1` 门面目录、 「症状 → 探针」对照表、`SceneSpace` 的不变量、改代码时的检查清单。 * [`docs/PLAN-stage-render.md`](docs/PLAN-stage-render.md) —— **舞台渲染与空气墙优化计划**。 现状基线、按域的优化项（P0/P1/P2）、四期路线与可跑验收指标。 * [`docs/ASSETS.md`](docs/ASSETS.md) —— **资产、库与美术方向**（一手来源核验，2026-10-14）。 * [`docs/REFERENCES.md`](docs/REFERENCES.md) —— **参考实现地图**（2026-10-15）。 把 M4 的"难实现"逐条映射到本机可借鉴的具体文件（相机模式切换、实例化、样式收敛、标签、 拾取、3D 代码怎么测），并诚实标出**本地没有、仍需联网去 GitHub 找**的三块 （骨骼动画 / SDF 文字 / 后处理）。**动手做 M4 之前先读它，别重新调研。** 推荐的 CC0 资产包、角色动画三方案对比、three.js 生态库版本与许可、许可红线、 `VENDOR.md` 台账模板、相机/光照/调色板配方与性能预算。 * [`docs/BACKLOG.md`](docs/BACKLOG.md) —— 轮次任务队列（每小时的自动化轮次从这里取活）。 * [`docs/PROGRESS.md`](docs/PROGRESS.md) —— 轮次台账（每轮必须更新）。 五条不能违背的原则： 1. **server-authoritative** —— 模拟跑在 host，渲染层只画状态、只发意图。面板关掉世界照跑。 2. **代码是机制，内容是数据** —— 凡可替换的东西一律进内容库；代码里**禁止**字面量的资产名、 剪辑名、任务文案、配色值。判据：问自己"这东西会不会有人想换掉"。 覆盖别人的条目必须**显式**声明 `overrides`，否则报错且原条目不变。 3. **`tick` 是纯函数 + seeded PRNG** —— 确定性 ⇒ 可回放 bug、可无 mock 测试。 模拟层**禁止** `Math.random()` 与 `Date.now()`。 4. **capability 落位** —— 任务只声明"需要什么能力"（`code` / `review` / `compute`…）， 不硬绑工位 ⇒ 小镇布局与任务编排解耦。 5. **模块之间只通过 `protocol/` 通信** —— 端口（进程内）/ 线协议（跨进程）/ 边界规则（依赖方向）。 **不是口号**：`test/boundaries.test.js` 读源码解析 import 逐条判定，违规即红。 三条最关键的：`sim/` 不许 import `content/`、`tools/` 只许 import `protocol/`、`web/` 只许 import `protocol/`。 分层依赖**单向向上**，不许出现环： ``` domain/（世界模型，不认识内容） ← content/（内容库与注册表） ← world/（装配：createWorld） ``` ## 路线图 | 阶段 | 内容 | |---|---| | **M0** ✅ | 骨架 + 世界模型类型 + 工具 + 测试 | | **M1** ✅ | **内容库层**：十个库的类型与校验、注册表（提供方链 / 显式覆盖）、内置内容包 | | **M1.5** | 外部内容包 ✅（`contentDir` 指过去即生效） | | **M1.6** | **契约层** ✅：端口 / 线协议 / 边界规则 + 强制检查 | | M2 | 模拟内核：`step()` 纯函数 tick、依赖求值、调度器、移动、邮箱、确定性验收 | | M3 | 落盘（`world.json`）+ HTTP 快照 + SSE 事件流（带 `seq` gap 自愈） | | M4 | three.js 场景：小镇、站点、相机、光照（消费 `themes`/`skins`/`districts`/`stations` 库） | | M5 | 角色、网格寻路、动画状态机（消费 `models`/`actions` 库；换 Kenney CC0 资产作验收） | | M6 | HUD：任务板 / 花名册 / 时间线 / 控制条 | | M7 | Bridge：接真实 subagent | | M8 | 打磨：美术 / 音效 / 后处理 / 性能降级 / 第二个主题包 | | M9 | 打包 / 文档 / 发布 | ## 开发 ```bash cd packages/dsh-agent-world # 本包**独立安装**，不走根 workspace。 # 原因：根 `pnpm install` 被 packages/dsh-daily 的过期 RC 版本钉死（与本包无关）， # 详见 docs/PROGRESS.md 的 R1「卡住」一节。 pnpm install --ignore-workspace --lockfile=false # 所有 pnpm run 都要带这个环境变量，否则 run 前的依赖校验会去跑根 install 并失败。 PNPM_CONFIG_VERIFY_DEPS_BEFORE_RUN=false pnpm run typecheck PNPM_CONFIG_VERIFY_DEPS_BEFORE_RUN=false pnpm test PNPM_CONFIG_VERIFY_DEPS_BEFORE_RUN=false pnpm run build ``` ## 配置 | 键 | 默认 | 说明 | |---|---|---| | `worldName` | `Agent World` | 默认世界名（也是 seed 来源：同名同场景 ⇒ 同一座小镇） | | `scene` | `scene.default-town` | 默认用哪个场景（`scenes` 库的 id）。**换它 = 换一座小镇，代码不动** | | `contentDir` | 空 | 外部内容包目录。留空 = 只用内置内容；绝对路径原样用；相对路径按宿主工作目录解析。实际路径会打进日志 | | `allowImplicitOverride` | `false` | 是否允许外部包隐式覆盖同 id 条目。默认关——"覆盖必须显式"是护栏 | | `tickMs` | `100` | 逻辑 tick 间隔。渲染层做插值，所以 10Hz 足够 | | `autoStart` | `true` | 插件加载后是否自动推进模拟 | | `maxAgents` | `24` | 同屏角色上限（性能预算的一部分） | | `stateDir` | `.agent-world` | 世界状态落盘目录（`//`）。M3 开始使用 | | `routePrefix` | `/agent-world` | 面板与 API 的路由前缀。M3 开始使用 | ## 目录 ``` src/protocol/ 契约层：boundaries（边界规则）/ ports（端口）/ wire（线协议 + codec） format（词汇表）/ format-text（排版）/ library-kinds —— 模块间唯一的通信面 src/content/ 内容库层：kinds / validate / registry / instantiate / packs / port（端口实现） src/domain/ 世界模型（纯逻辑：类型 / 数值调参 / rng / geometry / summary）——不认识"内容" src/world/ 装配：createWorld（内容 → World）+ 后续的 sim/ src/sim/ 模拟内核（M2，还没写） src/tools/ agent_world_* 工具 src/config.ts 配置 + resolveConfig 兜底 src/state.ts 插件态（内容注册表 + 当前世界） web/ 3D 面板（M4，还没写）—— Vite + three.js，独立构建，产物进 lib/web/ docs/ ARCHITECTURE / CONTENT / PROTOCOL / ASSETS / BACKLOG / PROGRESS test/ node --test ``` ## 许可 MIT。所有第三方美术资产只用 CC0/public domain，并逐个登记在 `web/public/assets/VENDOR.md`（来源 URL + 许可 + sha256），许可原文一并入库。 运行期**不依赖任何 CDN**。 ## ⚠️ 为什么 `package.json` 里有 `private: true` `src/vendor/microverse/` 的美术来自 **LimeZu Modern Office**，其条款明确 **"You CAN'T resell or distribute the asset to others"**（可用、不可分发）。 而 `files` 里的 `lib` 会把这套图一起打包。 `private: true` 是一个**防手滑**的闸：它让 `npm publish` 失败，这样"分发"必须由人**主动去掉这一行**才会发生。 署名已按对方要求补在 `CREDITS.md`（满足 "Credits required"），但**署名不能替代分发授权**。 **用户已知情并决定继续开发**（R59："不需要授权你只管搞就是了"），所以这不是阻塞项。 将来真要对外发布，先读 `docs/ASSET-LICENSES-EVIDENCE.md`（逐套原文证据）与 BACKLOG 的 M13-9。 # DSH Plugins Plugins for **DeepSeek Harness** (`dsh`) — one package per plugin, in a pnpm monorepo. Every package installs into a dsh profile on its own; this workspace exists so several plugins can be developed, built and dogfooded side by side. - Repository: - 中文文档: [README.zh.md](README.zh.md) ## Plugins `Add` is the argument to `dsh plugin --profile web add …` — see [Install](#install). | Package | What it does | Add | npm | Docs | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `dsh-agent-world`
`0.1.0` | Multi-agent collaboration in a visual **3D town**: every real subagent is a walking character, every task a pickable work order, every dispatch a move through space. Content libraries, a module protocol and the simulation core are in place; what ships today is a 2D top-down debug view — the 3D scene is not wired up yet. | `file:packages/dsh-agent-world` | not published (`private`) | [README](packages/dsh-agent-world/README.md) | | `dsh-contract-butler`
`0.1.0` | A contract keeper: extracts boundary contracts (the shape of inputs and outputs) back out of the code, watches them evolve across versions, and checks declared shapes against real runtime payloads — so "AI writes the implementation, humans own the agreement" has one reviewable source of truth. | `file:packages/dsh-contract-butler` | not published | [README](packages/dsh-contract-butler/README.md) | | `@kpeace/dsh-daily`
`0.10.4` | A **daily news digest** that recommends proactively, is tunable in natural language, indexes both articles and videos (YouTube / Bilibili), and lives in the right sidebar as a real web page — click an item and you are there. | `@kpeace/dsh-daily` | 0.10.4 | [README](packages/dsh-daily/README.md) | | `dsh-dev-git-graph`
`0.1.4` | A **Git Graph panel** in every conversation tab — a faithful port of [mhutchie/vscode-git-graph](https://github.com/mhutchie/vscode-git-graph) 1.30.0, auto-bound to the current session's workspace, with the commit graph (branch lanes, messages, dates, authors, refs) and the extension's full set of git operations on right-click. | `dsh-dev-git-graph` | 0.1.3 (this repo is at 0.1.4, unpublished) | [README](packages/dsh-dev-git-graph/README.md) | | `dsh-feishu`
`0.20.1` | Feishu (Lark) sync: configure your own authorization, and tasks and documents are synced locally on a schedule; a synced task can be opened directly as a DSH session, and progress, expectations and collaboration results are written back to Feishu. | `file:packages/dsh-feishu` | not published (`private`; the `dsh-feishu` name on npm belongs to an unrelated package) | [README](packages/dsh-feishu/README.md) | | `dsh-ios-skin`
`0.3.0` | An **iOS 26 Liquid Glass** theme for the DSH Web GUI — the official design tokens retuned plus a real frosted-material layer, with light/dark, reduced-transparency and high-contrast support. The current release is "Deep Fusion". | `dsh-ios-skin` | 0.1.0 (this repo is at 0.3.0, unpublished) | [README](packages/dsh-ios-skin/README.md) | | `dsh-mermaid-comm`
`0.3.1` | Makes the AI **default to Mermaid diagrams** in development conversations: a checkbox in the chat input controls prompt guidance, `mermaid_validate` checks syntax, an output gate repairs or removes broken diagrams, and a Mermaid vault versions them in the workspace. Rendering is handled by [`dsh-mermaid`](https://github.com/MrmoLabs/dsh-mermaid). | `dsh-mermaid-comm` (+ `dsh-mermaid`) | 0.3.1 | [README](packages/dsh-mermaid-comm/README.md) | | `dsh-spellbook`
`0.2.5` | The **spellbook**: a front-end effects library as a "Spellbook" right-sidebar tab. Each spell is a description of a mechanism plus code that really runs (the previews are live code, not recordings); one click sends a spell into the chat input, and the model can look one up with `spellbook_lookup`. | `dsh-spellbook` | 0.2.5 | [README](packages/dsh-spellbook/README.md) | | `dsh-tab-split`
`0.1.0` | **Conversation view split**: adds a "split" view tab that arranges resident views (chat / Git graph / …) into side-by-side panes. The official single view stays the default — nothing changes until you press the split button. | `file:packages/dsh-tab-split` | not published | [README](packages/dsh-tab-split/README.md) | | `dsh-example-tool`
`0.1.0` | The **minimal tool-plugin example**: registers `example_git_status` and `example_echo` with `defineTool`, and demonstrates the plugin module contract, config schema, and `output` / `render` declarations. Start here when writing a new plugin. | `file:packages/example-tool` | not published | [README](packages/example-tool/README.md) | ## Install ```bash # install one plugin into a profile (web in the examples) dsh plugin --profile web add # remove it dsh plugin --profile web remove # restart dsh (or reload the plugin) so the new entry is picked up ``` - **From npm**: pass the npm name (`dsh plugin --profile web add @kpeace/dsh-daily`). - **From a clone**: pass a path, e.g. `dsh plugin --profile web add file:packages/dsh-contract-butler` when run from the repository root (an absolute `file:/…` path works too). - **Whole workspace at once**: `pnpm build && pnpm install:web` builds every package and installs all of them into the `web` profile; `pnpm remove:web` takes them back out. - **Try things out in a throwaway profile** instead of your real one: `dsh plugin --profile devtest add `, then `dsh --profile devtest`. - A few packages document their own install path because they need something extra — check the package README before installing: `dsh-daily` (must be installed as a real directory, not a symlink), `dsh-feishu` (enable its bundle and authenticate the Feishu CLI), `dsh-dev-git-graph` (depends on `dsh-better-sidebar`), `dsh-mermaid-comm` (pairs with `dsh-mermaid`). ## Repository layout | Path | What it is | | --- | --- | | `packages//` | One directory per plugin — this is the layout and it is stable. Each package owns its `package.json`, `src/`, build output (`lib/`), assets and `README.md`. | | `package.json` | Workspace root: aggregated scripts (`build` / `typecheck` / `install:web` / …). | | `pnpm-workspace.yaml` | The pnpm workspace, `packages/*`. | | `tsconfig.base.json` | Shared TypeScript baseline for the packages. | | `docs/` | Directory and development conventions, the dsh plugin API reference, per-plugin design notes. | | `scripts/` | Install / remove / sync / scaffold helpers, plus the Desktop compatibility check. | | `templates/` | The `tool-plugin` template used by `scripts/new-plugin.sh`. | A package only ever lives at `packages/`, and its `package.json` name is what the profile resolves — helper output (`pnpm build` → `lib/`) never moves the source. ## Development The workspace is an **independent pnpm workspace**, not the dsh profile's own `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. Packages resolve dependencies and joint-debug here during development; release and installation go through `dsh plugin --profile add ` into `$DSH_HOME/profiles/`. If a package must be referenced by dsh as a `file:` dependency you could merge the profile directory in, but that drags the whole web app's dependency graph along — keep it separate. Node.js >= 22. ```bash pnpm install # resolve workspace dependencies pnpm build # build every package (pnpm -r run build) pnpm typecheck # type-check every package pnpm install:web # build and install all packages into the web profile ``` | Command | What it does | | --- | --- | | `pnpm build` | Build all plugin packages (each package emits `lib/` via `tsc` and copies its assets). | | `pnpm typecheck` | Type-check all plugin packages. | | `pnpm install:web` | Build and install all plugins into the `web` profile. | | `pnpm sync:web` | Copy build output into the `web` profile, including new files the hard-linked copies do not have. | | `pnpm sync:web:check` | Check only: exits 1 when a copy differs from source. | | `pnpm remove:web` | Remove all plugins from the `web` profile. | | `pnpm reinstall:web` | Reinstall (for iterative joint debugging). | | `pnpm --filter run dev` | Watch build for a single plugin. | | `bash scripts/new-plugin.sh my-plugin` | Scaffold a new plugin package from `templates/`. | | `pnpm dev:site` / `build:site` / `test:site` | Preview / build / test the spellbook site. | Two conventions worth knowing before you edit anything: - **New files need `pnpm sync:web`.** The profile holds hard-linked copies, so a file you add after the last sync does not appear there until you sync again. - **`peerDependencies` are the compatibility gate.** On DSH Desktop (Electron), plugins that declare a `@deepseek-ai/dsh*` range rejecting the current runtime are silently `disabled` before the profile starts — the symptom is "my plugin disappeared", not an error. Check a profile with `node scripts/verify-desktop-plugin-gate.mjs`; it calls the App's production `evaluatePluginCompatibility()`, so it does not drift from real behaviour. ## Conventions and references - [Directory conventions](docs/DIRECTORY.md) - [Development conventions](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md) — plugin lifecycle, module contract, profile strategy, quality red lines - [dsh plugin API reference](docs/REFERENCE.md)
